docs.title: 心理测量与 Test Development
docs.text: 本专题围绕心理与教育测验从“写出一道题”到“得到一个可解释分数”的完整链条展开。重点不是背诵孤立定义，而是学习如何判断一个项目（item）是否测到了目标构念、如何建立透明的评分规则，以及如何处理敏感问题中的反应偏差。

docs.title: 学习目标
docs.text:
完成本专题后，应当能够：

  1. 使用目的、目标群体、构念、题型、反应量表、公平性与反应偏差等维度批判项目质量。
  2. 识别含糊措辞、多重否定、双重问题、时间框架缺失和社会赞许性偏差。
  3. 区分整体式评分（holistic scoring）与分析式评分（analytic scoring），并写出带行为锚点的 rubric。
  4. 比较 Mark-M 多选题的不同计分算法，说明每种算法奖励或惩罚了什么作答行为。
  5. 建立随机化反应方案（randomized response scheme, RRS）的概率模型，并推导比例估计量、标准误和样本量要求。

docs.title: 专题内容
docs.text:
• Homework 1：项目编写、分析式评分与随机化反应

这篇讲义按照作业题目逐题组织。每道题都包含课程页码、核心术语、概念解释、常见误区、改写或计算示例，以及可追溯参考资料。

课程资料的使用方式

本站记录课程幻灯片的文件名与页码，方便在合法取得的课程资料中定位。课程幻灯片与作业原件不随公开网站再分发。

docs.title: Homework 1：项目编写、分析式评分与随机化反应
docs.text:
本页以 Homework 1 的题目结构组织课程知识。每一题都先抄录作业题干，再给出对应的课件原话短摘录、逐个术语的中英定义、概念之间的关系、答题逻辑与必要计算。它是一份学习讲义，不是可以直接提交的代写答案。

如何区分原话与讲解

“作业题干”来自老师发布的 Homework 1；“课件原话”只保留与本题最直接相关的短句，并附课件页码；其后的中文解释、例子和判断是依据课程原则展开的讲解。课件没有公布这份作业的逐题标准答案，因此本页不会把推导写成“老师的标准答案”。

docs.title: 作业与课程内容总图
docs.text:
作业部分 主要知识 课程材料定位 第 1 题 a--f 项目质量、措辞、题型、反应量表、公平性与反应偏差 WK1 pp. 6--7；WK2 pp. 10--20；DeVellis & Thorpe, Chapter 5, pp. 98--118 第 2 题 分析式评分、行为锚点、halo effect、评分者一致性 WK1 pp. 7, 10, 13--14；WK3 pp. 1, 11 第 3 题 Mark-M 多选题、部分计分、错误惩罚、评分规则 WK2 p. 15；WK3 pp. 1--2 第 4 题 系统偏差、社会赞许性、RRS、二项分布、估计量与精度 WK3 pp. 10, 14--18

第 1 题的稳妥答题句型

对每个 item 依次写四件事：判断（good / problematic）→ 术语 → 为什么影响测量 → 如何改写。只说“题目不好”通常不足以获得完整分数。

docs.title: 第 1 题：这些是不是好的 items？
docs.text:
第 1 题总题干 / Question 1 prompt

Read the following items. Based on what you have learned in this class, please explain if you think these items are good items. If not, please explain why and how would you improve them?

docs.title: 1(a) Tom Brady 与 Deflategate
docs.text:
作业题干 / Assignment prompt

To you does it seem likely or unlikely that Tom Brady was not involved in the deflate gate?

Likely / Unlikely

课件原话 / Slide wording

WK1 p. 6 把 “Response Bias” 列为五个 measurement problems 之一；WK1 p. 7 要求写题前明确 “Target population”、“Latent construct(s)” 和 “Item type”。这些短句没有直接判定本题对错，但给出了检查题目的三个入口：谁作答、要测什么、用什么反应形式。

课程定位

  • WK1 p. 6：measurement scale 与 response bias。
  • WK1 p. 7：target population、cross-cultural usage、item type。
  • WK2 p. 12：attitude items 的 selected-response formats。
  • DeVellis & Thorpe, pp. 99--102：clarity、multiple negatives、negatively worded items。

核心术语

术语 English 完整含义 在本题中怎么看 项目／题目 item 向被试呈现、要求产生一个可计分反应的最小测量单位 这里包括题干和 Likely/Unlikely 两个选项 题干 item stem 告诉被试要判断什么的文字部分 “was not involved” 是题干中的否定核心 否定措辞 negative wording 用 not、never、unlikely 等否定形式表达命题 题干有 not，反应词又有 unlikely，方向容易反转 复杂否定 complex or multiple negation 理解答案时必须连续处理两个或更多否定方向 “unlikely that ... was not involved” 不能按单个词直接映射 含糊性 ambiguity 同一措辞允许多个合理解释或反应方向 Likely 到底是在评价“参与”还是“未参与”，容易读错 二分反应 binary response 只有两个可选结果的反应格式 它不能表达不确定程度，也不能区分中立与不了解事件 筛选项 filter or screening option 先判断被试是否具备回答后续题所需经验或知识 “Not familiar enough to answer” 可避免不了解事件者被迫猜测 构念无关难度 construct-irrelevant difficulty 作答难度来自目标构念之外的语言、记忆或背景知识 复杂否定和 Deflategate 背景知识都可能污染态度测量 反应偏差 response bias 与真实构念水平无关、却系统改变回答的倾向 若某类被试更容易被否定方向误导，误差可能具有系统性

题干一边要求判断 “likely or unlikely”，一边又询问 “was not involved”。被试必须先理解事件、再处理否定、最后把判断映射到 likely/unlikely，容易发生方向性错误。这种额外认知负担不是目标态度本身，因此会增加构念无关误差。

二分选项也压缩了态度强度，而且没有为不熟悉事件的人提供 “Don’t know / Not familiar enough to answer”。强迫这些人猜测会把背景知识混入态度分数。

一种更清楚的改写

How likely do you think it is that Tom Brady was involved in Deflategate?

Very unlikely / Unlikely / Neither likely nor unlikely / Likely / Very likely / Not familiar enough to answer

改写去掉了否定，增加有序程度选项，并把“不具备作答信息”与真正的中立态度分开。

docs.title: 1(b) Compensation and benefits
docs.text:
作业题干 / Assignment prompt

I am satisfied with my compensation and benefits package.

Strongly disagree / Disagree / Neutral / Agree / Strongly Agree

课件原话 / Slide wording

WK2 p. 12 的 job-satisfaction 示例只问一个判断对象：“I feel I am being paid a fair amount for the work I do.” 这为本题提供了对照：一个态度 item 应让一次反应对应一个清楚主张。

课程定位

  • WK2 p. 12：Likert-type attitude item。
  • WK2 pp. 19--20：Are these good items?
  • DeVellis & Thorpe, p. 100：double-barreled items。

核心术语

术语 English 完整含义 在本题中怎么看 双重问题 double-barreled item 一个题干同时询问两个可能得到不同答案的对象或主张 compensation 与 benefits 可能一个满意、一个不满意 潜在构念 latent construct 不能直接观察、需通过多个反应推断的心理属性 “job satisfaction” 需要由一组项目代表，而非由措辞含混的一题决定 单维性 unidimensionality 一组项目的主要共同变化可由一个主导维度解释 拆题后仍要检验薪酬满意和福利满意是否属于同一可合成维度 Likert 型项目 Likert-type item 单个陈述配有按同意程度排序的反应类别 本题是单个 Likert-type item；多个此类项目合成后才通常称为 Likert scale 中点 neutral midpoint 反应量表中代表中立、两可或无方向的位置 Neutral 不应被用来替代“对工资和福利意见相反” 反应映射 response mapping 被试把内部判断转换到给定选项的过程 两个对象只有一个按钮，使内部的两个判断无法无损映射 测量误差 measurement error 观察分数与目标属性之间的偏离 被迫折中会给答案加入与真实满意度无关的误差

该 item 同时询问 compensation 和 benefits。一个人可能满意工资但不满意福利，此时任何单一选项都会误表其至少一个态度。问题不在于 Likert 量表本身，而在于一个题干包含两个可能分离的判断对象。

改写原则：一题只测一个主张

I am satisfied with my compensation.

I am satisfied with my benefits package.

如果两题将来要合成同一分数，还需要用项目分析检验它们是否确实反映同一潜在构念。

docs.title: 1(c) Corporal punishment 的频率
docs.text:
作业题干 / Assignment prompt

How often do you use corporal punishment on your children at home?

Never / Seldom / Occasionally / Sometimes / Often / Very Often / All the time

课件原话 / Slide wording

WK3 p. 14 在 “Social desirability” 下给出两种处理方向，其中之一是 “use randomized respondent scheme (RRS)”。WK1 p. 6 也把 “Response Bias” 单列为 measurement problem。

课程定位

  • WK1 p. 6：measurement scale 与 response bias。
  • WK3 p. 13：scale-use bias。
  • WK3 p. 14：social desirability。
  • WK3 pp. 15--18：randomized response scheme。
  • DeVellis & Thorpe, pp. 106--107：模糊的 response labels。
  • DeVellis & Thorpe, pp. 117--118：item time frame。

核心术语

术语 English 完整含义 在本题中怎么看 敏感项目 sensitive item 诚实回答可能带来羞耻、污名、惩罚或隐私风险的题目 corporal punishment 受社会规范约束，少报风险高 社会赞许性偏差 social-desirability bias 为呈现更符合社会期待的形象而系统性改变回答 被试可能选择比实际更低的频率 模糊量词 vague quantifier 没有固定数值边界的频率词，如 seldom、often 不同人对 occasionally 与 sometimes 的理解可能相反 类别重叠 overlapping categories 两个选项可以同时覆盖同一真实状态 “Seldom / Occasionally / Sometimes” 没有互斥边界 互斥性 mutual exclusivity 任一真实答案最多落入一个反应类别 用 0、1、2--3、4--5、6+ 可减少重叠 穷尽性 exhaustiveness 所有合理状态至少有一个可选类别 需要加入“没有孩子／不适用”等选项 参照期 reference period or time frame 题目要求回忆行为的明确时间窗口 “过去 30 天”比无限期的 “how often” 更可比 行为具体化 behavioral specificity 用可观察动作代替抽象、价值化标签 应说明是 spank、strike，还是包括其他行为 随机化反应方案 randomized response scheme, RRS 借助已知随机机制隐藏个体真实状态，再估计群体比例 适合降低敏感行为问题的系统性少报

该题涉及受社会规范约束的敏感行为，被试可能少报以维持正面形象，产生系统性偏差。“Seldom”“Occasionally”“Sometimes”没有公共、稳定的数值含义，类别之间也可能重叠。此外，题干没有说明过去一周、一个月还是一生，也默认所有被试都有孩子并对 corporal punishment 有同一理解。

一种行为化改写

During the past 30 days, how many times did you intentionally spank or strike your child as punishment?

0 / 1 / 2--3 / 4--5 / 6 or more / I do not have a child

改写加入时间框架、可观察行为和互斥的数量类别。如果诚实作答仍然令人担忧，可以使用第 4 题所示的 RRS；它以更大的随机方差换取更强的个人隐私与较少的社会赞许性偏差。

docs.title: 1(d) Good intentions 与说谎
docs.text:
作业题干 / Assignment prompt

It is acceptable to lie as long as you have good intentions.

Strongly disagree / Disagree / Neutral / Agree / Strongly Agree

课件原话 / Slide wording

WK2 p. 19 把 “All hand-guns should be licensed because ...” 放在 “Are these good items” 的讨论中。它与本题结构相似：先给一个态度主张，再用 because/as long as 加入可能影响判断的理由或条件。

课程定位

  • WK2 pp. 19--20：Are these good items?
  • WK3 p. 14：social desirability。
  • DeVellis & Thorpe, pp. 99--101：ambiguity、conditional wording、double-barreled items。

核心术语

术语 English 完整含义 在本题中怎么看 条件性措辞 conditional wording 用 if、unless、as long as 等条件限制主命题 回答同时取决于“说谎”和“good intentions”两个判断 含糊性 ambiguity 关键概念没有足够清楚、共同的解释边界 lie、acceptable、good intentions 都可能指不同情境 评价性用语 evaluative language 词语自身带有正负价值暗示 good 已经暗示动机值得赞许，可能推动同意 诱导性项目 leading item 措辞使某个答案显得更合理、正常或被期待 “good intentions” 可能替谎言提供预设辩护 构念表征 construct representation 项目集合对目标构念各重要成分的覆盖程度 单一“善意谎言”场景不能代表一般的 lying permissiveness 内容抽样 content sampling 从理论上可能无限的行为与情境中抽取有限项目 需要多种清楚情境，才能减少一个例子决定整体分数的问题 社会赞许性偏差 social-desirability bias 回答受“我希望别人怎样看我”影响，而非只受真实态度影响 有人可能为了显得诚实而不同意，也可能为了显得善良而同意

“acceptable”“lie”和“good intentions”都可能被不同被试理解为不同事件。“as long as”又把对说谎的判断与对动机的判断绑定起来。被试想到善意谎言、隐瞒疾病、学术不诚实或保护他人的谎言时，可能给出完全不同的反应。

一种更具体的改写

It is acceptable to withhold distressing information temporarily when doing so is intended to protect another person.

即使如此，一个 item 也只抽取了有限的行为情境。如果目标是测量一般性的 lying permissiveness，应写多个清楚且覆盖不同情境的 items，再研究其内部结构。

docs.title: 1(e) Extinct animal 生物题
docs.text:
作业题干 / Assignment prompt

An example of an extinct animal is an ...

A. sloth

B. eskimo curlew

C. pigeon

D. chimpanzee

课件原话 / Slide wording

WK2 p. 10 强调 “Selecting an appropriate item format ... for the intended population”；WK3 p. 1 把 “Correct/Incorrect” 和 “Formula scoring” 列为 optimal-performance item 的计分选择。二者都预设标准答案必须能清楚辩护。

课程定位

  • WK2 pp. 11, 13：optimal-performance tests 与 multiple-choice format。
  • WK3 p. 1：correct/incorrect、formula scoring 与 partial credit。

核心术语

术语 English 完整含义 在本题中怎么看 最佳表现测验 optimal-performance test 要求被试展示其最高知识或能力水平、存在对错标准的测验 生物知识题属于 optimal performance，而非态度自陈 选择题 multiple-choice item 由题干、一个或多个正确选项及干扰项构成的 selected-response item 本题预期只有一个最佳答案 标准答案 key or keyed option 依据内容和评分规则被指定为正确的选项 key 必须在目标课程知识和时间点上无争议 干扰项 distractor 不正确但对知识不足者具有一定吸引力的选项 distractor 应明确错误，不能因分类范围含混而“部分正确” 选项同质性 option homogeneity 各选项在语法、类别层级和表述粒度上相似 宽泛动物类别与具体物种混用会暴露线索或制造歧义 唯一最佳答案 single best answer 在题干规定下只有一个选项可被最充分辩护 若 pigeon 可指 passenger pigeon，原题就可能不再唯一 内容效度 content validity 项目内容能否充分、恰当地代表拟测知识领域 题目分类学边界不清会削弱“答对代表掌握生物知识”的解释

知识测验的标准答案必须可以明确辩护。原题混合了宽泛动物类别与具体物种名称；某些宽泛类别同时包含现存与灭绝成员，而较少见物种的分类状态也可能造成争议。这样一来，答错可能反映题目边界不清，而非生物知识不足。

一种更稳妥的改写

Which of the following species is extinct?

A. Dodo

B. Chimpanzee

C. Bald eagle

D. Blue whale

改写后的选项处于相近的分类层级，只有一个明确的 keyed answer，其余选项是合理但明确错误的 distractors。

docs.title: 1(f) 美国硬币数学题
docs.text:
作业题干 / Assignment prompt

You have a quarter, three pennies, two dimes, and four nickels. How much money in total do you have in cents?

课件原话 / Slide wording

WK2 p. 4 将 fairness 描述为尽量 “minimize barriers to valid score interpretations”，并提出通过 accommodations “remove construct-irrelevant barriers”。WK1 p. 7 同时要求先考虑 “Target population” 与 “Cross cultural usage”。

课程定位

  • WK1 p. 7：target population 与 cross-cultural usage。
  • WK2 p. 4：fairness 与 construct-irrelevant barriers。
  • WK2 p. 10：item format 必须适合 intended population。

核心术语

术语 English 完整含义 在本题中怎么看 公平性 fairness 设计、施测和解释应尽量让分数反映目标构念，而非无关障碍 同样会加法的人不应只因不认识美国硬币名称而失分 目标群体 target population 分数解释希望推广到的被试总体 若对象是美国小学且已教过硬币，要求可能合理；跨国群体则未必 文化负载 cultural loading 作答依赖特定文化经验、制度或常识的程度 quarter、dime、nickel 是美国文化与语言知识 语言需求 linguistic demand 理解与表达题目所需的词汇、句法和阅读能力 当目标仅为加法时，硬币词汇属于额外阅读需求 构念无关方差 construct-irrelevant variance 分数差异由不在目标构念定义内的因素产生 不熟悉币值造成的失分污染 arithmetic score 调整措施 accommodation 在不改变目标构念的前提下移除无关障碍 可给硬币图示或币值；若“识币”属于构念则不应提供 测试蓝图 test blueprint 事先规定内容、认知要求、题型与权重的设计表 蓝图必须说明本题究竟测加法、货币知识，还是两者 预期分数用途 intended score use 分数将支持的具体解释或决策 同一题用于课堂练习和全国性高风险决策，公平性要求不同

如果目标构念是整数加法，原题还要求知道 quarter、penny、dime 和 nickel 的名称与币值。对不熟悉美国货币或英语词汇的学生，错误可能来自文化知识而非算术能力。此时分数解释受到 construct-irrelevant variance 污染。

改写取决于测试目的

  • 若测算术：直接询问 (25+3+20+20)。
  • 若测现实货币运用：保留硬币，但在 blueprint 中明确“识别美国币值”属于构念，并确认目标群体接受过相应教学。
  • 若希望降低语言障碍：展示硬币图像及币值，而不是只给名称。

docs.title: 第 2 题：分析式评分量规
docs.text:
作业题干 / Assignment prompt

A department asks faculty in each area to evaluate their graduate students and provide informative feedback to them. Our department does not do this, but suppose the department asks faculty to place each student in three performance categories. Please come up with a scoring rubric following the analytical approach.

课件原话 / Slide wording

WK3 p. 1 强调评分是 “a separate facet of item/scale development”。WK3 p. 11 对 halo effect 的核心表述是，局部判断可能 “be influenced by one’s overall impression”。因此，量规不仅要给三个标签，还要把总体印象拆成可独立观察和评分的维度。

docs.title: 2.1 Analytical 与 holistic 的区别
docs.text:
课程定位

  • WK1 p. 7：先明确 purpose、target population 与 latent construct。
  • WK1 p. 10：construct domain、blueprint、item review 与 pilot。
  • WK1 pp. 13--14：content coverage、task analysis 与 subject-matter experts。
  • WK3 p. 1：scoring 是 item/scale development 的独立环节。
  • WK3 p. 11：halo effect。

整体式评分（holistic scoring）要求评分者形成一个总体印象；分析式评分（analytic scoring）先把表现拆成明确维度，逐维评分，再按事先规定的规则合成结果。分析式方法使评分依据更透明，也可减少 halo effect：评分者不应因为对学生的总体好感而让所有维度同时偏高。

docs.title: 2.2 术语逐个解释
docs.text: 术语 English 完整含义 在本题中的操作化 评分量规 scoring rubric 把评价维度、表现等级、行为描述和合成规则预先写明的评分工具 faculty 应依据共同量规，而非各自凭感觉分类 评价维度 criterion or dimension 需要分别观察和判断的表现方面 可设 research、methodology、professional performance 三维 表现等级 performance level 每个维度上有序的质量类别 Needs improvement、Meets、Exceeds 构成三等级 分析式评分 analytic scoring 逐维给分，再依明确规则形成总分或类别 学生可看出具体优势和改进点，反馈信息更多 整体式评分 holistic scoring 根据总体印象一次给出总等级 快，但不容易说明为何被分入某类 行为锚点 behavioral anchor 用可观察、可核实的行为说明某个分数代表什么 “按时提交可复现分析”比“表现很好”更可评分 光环效应 halo effect or halo error 对人的总体印象系统性影响对多个局部特征的判断 觉得某学生聪明，可能连合作、严谨性也都打高 评分者间信度 inter-rater reliability 不同评分者对同一表现给出一致结果的程度 多位 faculty 应对同一案例得到接近的维度分数 评分者校准 rater calibration 用样例、讨论和反馈建立共同使用标准的过程 正式评分前共同练习边界案例 内容效度 content validity 量规维度能否充分代表培养目标和拟评价能力 维度应来自 graduate program outcomes 与 SMEs 证据记录 evidence record 支撑每个维度判断的具体作品、行为或观察 每个评分旁记录论文、分析、报告或合作证据 补偿式规则 compensatory rule 一个维度的高分可以抵消另一维度的低分 直接相加的 3--9 分属于补偿式合成 合取式规则 conjunctive rule 每个关键维度都必须达到最低标准 若研究伦理不可被其他优点抵消，应设最低门槛

docs.title: 2.3 一个三等级 analytic rubric
docs.text:
评分维度 1 — Needs improvement 2 — Meets expectations 3 — Exceeds expectations Research and conceptual competence 理论或文献掌握不足；研究问题不清楚或与证据脱节 能准确解释主要理论并形成可行问题 能整合不同文献、识别缺口并提出有价值的新问题 Methodological competence 设计或分析存在重要错误，需要大量指导 能选择并执行基本合适的方法，主要结论有证据支持 能独立论证方法选择、检查假设并进行稳健性分析 Professional performance 经常延误；沟通、合作或研究记录不足 工作可靠、按时，沟通清楚并遵守研究规范 主动推进工作，独立性强，并能有效支持团队成员

将三个维度相加得到 3--9 分，再映射为三个最终类别：

  • 3--4：Needs improvement
  • 5--7：Meets expectations
  • 8--9：Exceeds expectations

docs.title: 2.4 一个合格 rubric 还需要什么？
docs.text:
• Behavioral anchors：每个等级描述可观察行为，而不是“good”“average”等循环定义。
  • Content validity：维度与权重必须来自项目培养目标和 faculty SMEs，而不是评分者临时决定。
  • Inter-rater reliability：多位教师应使用样例进行校准，并检查是否给出近似评分。
  • Evidence record：每个维度应记录支持判断的具体证据。
  • Decision rule：总分类阈值、缺失证据处理方式和是否允许某个关键维度补偿另一个维度，都要提前规定。

三等级不等于三个模糊标签

只有 “poor / average / good” 三个名称仍然是整体印象。分析式方法的关键是多个构念相关维度 + 每个维度的行为锚点 + 明确合成规则。

docs.title: 第 3 题：Mark-M 多选题的四种评分算法
docs.text:
作业题干 / Assignment prompt

A Mark-M item has 10 answer options. What are the following are the capital of a country?

Rio de Janeiro / New York / Santiago / Shanghai / Cape Town / Prague / Berlin / Dubai / Cairo / Barcelona

(a) What is your answer to this question? (This does not count towards your grade.)

(b) Come up with four scoring algorithms and explain their advantages and disadvantages.

(c) The correct answer is Santiago, Prague, Berlin and Cairo. All the other answers are incorrect (at least for now!). Use the four scoring mechanisms to score yourself given your answer in (a).

课件原话 / Slide wording

WK2 p. 15 把这种题型写成 “Pick K out of N; or multiple-mark items”，并说明 K 有时给出、有时不提供。WK3 p. 2 的表题为 “Different Scoring Algorithms for Mark-M Items”，列出 SA1--SA8；作业只要求选择四种并解释，而不是把八种全部用于自己的答案。

docs.title: 3.1 题型与符号
docs.text:
课程定位

  • WK2 p. 15：Pick \(K\) out of \(N\) 与 multiple-mark items。
  • WK3 p. 1：Mark-M、partial credit 与 scoring choices。
  • WK3 p. 2：八种 Mark-M scoring algorithms；本题要求自选并解释四种。

该题共有 10 个城市，其中 Santiago、Prague、Berlin 和 Cairo 为四个 keyed correct options。定义：

符号 课件英文 完整含义 本题中的值或关系 \(S\) respondent's score 该题最终得分；课件表中的上限设为 1 依所选 SA 而变 \(TO\) total number of item options 全部备选项数 \(TO=10\) \(CO\) number of keyed correct options 评分键中正确选项的数量 \(CO=4\) \(MCO=m\) correct options marked 被试实际选中的正确项数，即 hit 数 \(0\leq m\leq4\) \(MIO=i\) incorrect options marked 被试误选的干扰项数，即 false-positive 数 \(0\leq i\leq6\) \(CC\) correct choices 所有正确的二分判断：选中正确项加未选干扰项 \(CC=m+(6-i)\) \(IC\) incorrect choices 所有错误的二分判断：误选干扰项加漏选正确项 \(IC=i+(4-m)\) \(MO\) marked options 被试勾选的全部选项数，不论对错 \(MO=m+i\) \(x\) penalty 某些算法对过度勾选设置的惩罚量 只在采用相应算法时使用

表中的 option-level “choice” 是对每个选项作出的二分判断：应该选还是不应该选。因此，“没有选一个 distractor”属于 correct rejection，也计入 \(CC\)。

docs.title: 3.2 判断结果与术语全解
docs.text: 真实状态 × 作答 中文 English 本题含义 正确项且选中 命中 hit or true positive 应选的首都被选中 正确项但未选 漏选 miss or false negative 应选的首都被遗漏 错误项但选中 误选／假阳性 false positive 非首都被错误勾选 错误项且未选 正确拒绝 correct rejection or true negative 干扰项被正确留空 术语 English 完整含义 为什么重要 多重作答题 multiple-mark item 一个题干允许或要求选择多个选项 作答不是单一 A/B/C/D，而是一个选项向量 Pick \(K\) out of \(N\) select \(K\) of \(N\) 从 \(N\) 个选项中选 \(K\) 个；\(K\) 可告知或不告知 告知 \(K=4\) 会改变猜测策略和题目难度 选择反应 selected response 被试从预先给定的选项中选择，而非自由作答 评分依赖选项设计和 scoring key 二分计分 dichotomous scoring 整题只有 0/1 两个分值 exact match 属于这一类 部分计分 partial-credit scoring 不完全正确的反应模式仍可获得中间分 能保留“知道三个、漏一个”的信息 公式计分 formula scoring 依据命中、误选、漏选等数量用公式合成分数 不同公式实际上定义了不同的“掌握” 正确命中率 hit rate or sensitivity 所有正确项中被选中的比例 \(MCO/CO\)；只看发现正确项的能力 假阳性率 false-positive rate 所有错误项中被误选的比例 \(MIO/(TO-CO)\)；反映乱选或过度勾选 反应策略 response strategy 被试为最大化期望得分而采用的选或不选规则 惩罚太重可能让被试即使知道也不敢选 分数边界 score bounds 一个算法允许的最低和最高分 SA2、SA4 可能为负；报告时应说明是否截断

docs.title: 3.3 四种算法及其测量含义
docs.text:
算法 定义 奖励与惩罚 优点 局限 SA1 Exact match \(S=1\) if \(IC=0\)，否则 \(S=0\) 只有完全正确才得分 简单、严格、不产生策略性部分分 漏掉一个正确项也得 0，信息利用率低 SA2 Correct minus incorrect \(S=(CC-IC)/TO\) 奖励正确判断并对错误判断作对称惩罚 区分部分知识与完全错误 可出现负分；选项比例不平衡时策略行为较复杂 SA3 Proportion of correct decisions \(S=CC/TO\) 每个选项判断权重相同 直观、范围为 0--1 错误项多时，“全部不选”也可能得到较高分 SA4 Hit rate minus false-positive rate \(S=MCO/CO-MIO/(TO-CO)\) 平衡正确命中率和误选率 不让较多的 distractors 支配总分 可为负；对普通考生不如百分比直观

SA4 具有类似 sensitivity minus false-positive rate 的结构：

\[ S_{SA4} = \frac{\text{correct options selected}}{\text{all correct options}} - \frac{\text{incorrect options selected}}{\text{all incorrect options}}. \]

它区分“发现正确答案的能力”和“把错误答案误报为正确的倾向”。

课件为什么列出八种算法？

WK3 p. 2 还列出 SA5--SA8，说明 Mark-M 没有唯一自然计分法：有的加入 chance/penalty，有的只奖励命中，有的设置半分阈值。该页嵌入表在右侧和脚注处有截断，且没有给出原论文的完整书目信息；这里不猜补模糊符号。作业要求的四种算法以上述可清楚辨认的 SA1--SA4 完成。

docs.title: 3.4 用自己的答案计算四次
docs.text:
代入 \(TO=10\)、\(CO=4\)：

\[ S_{SA1}= \begin{cases} 1,&m=4\text{ and }i=0,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}, \end{cases} \] \[ S_{SA2}=\frac{m-i+1}{5}, \qquad S_{SA3}=\frac{m+6-i}{10}, \qquad S_{SA4}=\frac{m}{4}-\frac{i}{6}. \]

例如，只漏选 Cairo，另外三个正确城市都选中且没有误选，则 \(m=3,i=0\)：

算法 分数 SA1 \(0\) SA2 \(0.80\) SA3 \(0.90\) SA4 \(0.75\)

这组结果说明 scoring rule 不是最后的技术细节；它实质上定义了什么样的作答行为被视为“掌握”。

docs.title: 第 4 题：Randomized Response Scheme
docs.text:
作业题干 / Assignment prompt

An educational psychologist interested in investigating cheating behavior among high school students tries to get around social desirability by using the following scheme.

“Question: Have you ever cheated on any assignment or exam? Please flip a coin without showing it to anyone else. If you get a head, please answer truthfully. If you get tail, please answer untruthfully. Since I don't know whether you get a head or tail from the flip, I'll never know whether your answer is truthful or not; therefore, you do not need to worry about being identified as having cheated or not. Please circle your answer: Yes / No.”

(a) She collected data from 120 students. And she gave them loaded coins, with probability of head of .7, and probability of tail of .3. In the end she found that 80 students responded “yes” and 40 responded “no” to her question. Please estimate the percentage of students ever cheated on an assignment or exam.

(b) What if she collected data from 12 students, and 8 responded “yes”? What is your estimate of percentage of students ever cheated? Are you more confident in your estimate in a) or in b)? Why?

(c) Consider asking the question directly to the participants. Suppose out of the 120 participants, 80 students responded “yes” and 40 responded “no”. What is your estimate of the percentage of students ever cheated on an assignment or exam? Compared to the answer in a), is it lower or higher or the same?

(d) By using the RRS in a) you are supposed to get less biased estimate but your estimate has larger variability. In order to reach the same level of precision in your estimate as in c), how big a sample size you need at the minimum under the RRS in a)? Required for quant grad student only. Optional for others.

docs.title: 4.1 为什么要随机化？
docs.text:
课件原话 / Slide wording

WK3 p. 10 对 measurement error 写的是 “Random fluctuation”、“In the long run cancels itself out”；对 systematic bias 写的是 “Non-random”、“In the longrun accumulates”。WK3 p. 14 在 social desirability 下提出 “use randomized respondent scheme (RRS)”。

课程定位

  • WK3 p. 10：measurement error 与 systematic bias。
  • WK3 p. 14：social desirability。
  • WK3 p. 15：loaded-coin RRS 例题。
  • WK3 pp. 16--17：估计公式与 worked example。
  • WK3 p. 18：fair coin、小样本和个体判断等失败条件。

直接询问作弊、欺凌等敏感行为时，被试可能系统性少报。随机化反应方案让研究者不知道某个个体是否按真实状态回答，却仍能利用群体中随机装置的已知概率估计总体比例。

这体现了两个误差来源的权衡：

  • Systematic bias：非随机地把估计推向某个方向，长期不会抵消。
  • Random measurement/sampling error：在重复样本中上下波动，平均而言可以抵消，但会降低精度。

RRS 希望用更多随机误差换取更少的社会赞许性系统偏差。

docs.title: 4.2 概率模型与分布
docs.text:
术语 English 完整含义 本题中的角色 敏感特征 sensitive trait 被试可能因污名、惩罚或隐私风险而隐藏的真实状态 是否曾作弊是不可直接放心报告的二分状态 总体比例 prevalence or population proportion 总体中真实状态为 Yes 的成员比例 目标参数是 \(\pi\)，不是样本里的观察 Yes 比例 随机化反应方案 randomized response scheme, RRS 用研究者已知、个体结果未知的随机机制保护真实回答 抛硬币决定说真话还是说反话 负载硬币 loaded coin 正反面概率不相等的硬币或等价随机装置 \(p=.7\) 使 \(\pi\) 可被识别且保留一定隐私 潜在真实状态 latent true status 每个人实际是否具有敏感特征，研究者不可直接观察 记为 true cheating status 观察反应 observed response 经过随机规则后研究者实际看到的 Yes/No 其 Yes 概率是 \(\lambda\)，一般不等于 \(\pi\) Bernoulli 分布 Bernoulli distribution 单个二分随机变量的分布，取 1 的概率为 \(\lambda\) 每人的 observed Yes 指标 \(X_j\) 服从 Bernoulli 二项分布 Binomial distribution \(n\) 个独立同分布 Bernoulli 变量之和的分布 总 Yes 数 \(Y\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(n,\lambda)\) 参数 parameter 描述总体、固定但未知的量 \(\pi\) 与由机制决定的 \(\lambda\) 统计量 statistic 由样本数据计算出的随机量 \(Y\) 与 \(\hat\lambda=Y/n\) 估计量 estimator 用样本统计量估计未知参数的规则 \(\hat\pi=(\hat\lambda+p-1)/(2p-1)\) 偏差 bias 估计量长期平均值与目标参数之差 直接询问可能因隐瞒作弊而向下偏 方差 variance 估计量在重复样本中的波动平方尺度 RRS 的随机装置会放大方差 标准误 standard error, SE 估计量抽样分布标准差；等于方差平方根 用于比较 120 人与 12 人估计的稳定性 精度 precision 估计的随机波动大小；方差或 SE 越小越精确 第 4(d) 要把 RRS 精度提高到直接询问水平 可识别性 identifiability 观察分布能否唯一确定目标参数 \(p=.5\) 时不同 \(\pi\) 都给 \(\lambda=.5\)，所以不可识别 plug-in 估计 plug-in estimate 用样本估计值代替方差公式中的未知概率 第 4(d) 用 \(\hat\lambda=2/3\) 计算所需 \(n\)

令：

  • \(\pi\)：总体中真实有过作弊行为的比例；
  • \(p=0.7\)：硬币正面概率；正面时诚实回答；
  • \(1-p=0.3\)：反面概率；反面时说反话；
  • \(\lambda=P(\text{observed Yes})\)：最终观察到 Yes 的概率。

观察到 Yes 有两条互斥路径：真实作弊且得到正面，或者真实未作弊但得到反面并说反话。因此

\[ \lambda=p\pi+(1-p)(1-\pi). \]

每位被试的观察反应 \(X_j\) 服从 Bernoulli 分布，总 Yes 数 \(Y\) 服从 Binomial 分布：

\[ X_j\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\lambda), \qquad Y=\sum_{j=1}^{n}X_j\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,\lambda). \]

由上式解出 \(\pi\)：

\[ \hat\pi = \frac{\hat\lambda+p-1}{2p-1}, \qquad \hat\lambda=\frac Yn. \]

分母 \(2p-1\) 解释了为什么 fair coin 会使这一版本失败：当 \(p=0.5\) 时，分母为 0，观察到 Yes 的概率不再包含可识别的 \(\pi\) 信息。

docs.title: 4(a) 120 人中 80 人回答 Yes
docs.text:
\[ \hat\lambda=\frac{80}{120}=\frac23. \] \[ \hat\pi = \frac{\frac23+0.7-1}{2(0.7)-1} = \frac{0.3667}{0.4} \approx0.9167. \]

所以估计约 \(91.67\%\) 的学生曾经作弊。必须注意：\(80/120\) 是观察 Yes 比例，不是目标 prevalence；它混合了诚实回答与被迫说反话两条路径。

docs.title: 4(b) 12 人中 8 人回答 Yes
docs.text:
\(8/12\) 仍等于 \(2/3\)，所以点估计仍为 \(91.67\%\)。但是样本量只有原来的十分之一，估计明显更不稳定。

\[ \operatorname{Var}(\hat\pi) = \frac{\lambda(1-\lambda)}{n(2p-1)^2}, \] \[ SE(\hat\pi) = \sqrt{\frac{\hat\lambda(1-\hat\lambda)}{n(2p-1)^2}}. \]

当观察比例相同而 \(n\) 从 120 减为 12 时，标准误增大为原来的 \(\sqrt{10}\) 倍。因此对 4(a) 的估计更有信心。

docs.title: 4(c) 直接询问
docs.text:
直接询问时，观察 Yes 就被当作真实 Yes：

\[ \hat\pi_{\text{direct}}=\frac{80}{120}=0.6667. \]

它低于 RRS 的 \(0.9167\)。这并不自动证明 RRS 数字就是“真值”；概念重点是：直接询问的方差较小，但可能受社会赞许性偏差影响；RRS 增加方差，却为个体提供隐私并试图降低系统性低报。

docs.title: 4(d) 达到相同精度需要多大样本？
docs.text:
直接估计量的 plug-in 方差为

\[ \widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\pi_D) = \frac{(2/3)(1/3)}{120} = \frac{1}{540}. \]

若新的 RRS 样本仍使用 \(\hat\lambda=2/3\)，则

\[ \widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\pi_R) = \frac{(2/3)(1/3)}{n(0.4)^2} = \frac{25}{18n}. \]

令 RRS 方差不大于直接询问：

\[ \frac{25}{18n}\leq\frac{1}{540} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad n\geq750. \]

因此，在题目给定比例下，plug-in 解法要求至少 \(750\) 人。

样本量答案依赖比较假设

上面的 \(750\) 使用两种样本中各自观察到的 \(2/3\) 作为方差的 plug-in 概率。若课程要求在共同的真实 prevalence \(\pi=2/3\) 下比较两种设计，则 RRS 中 \(\lambda=0.3+0.4(2/3)=17/30\)，向上取整后得到 \(829\)。作答时应明确写出采用的假设；按题目现有观察比例，\(750\) 是最直接的答案。

docs.title: 4.3 何时不应使用这一版本？
docs.text:
• \(p=0.5\)：\(\pi\) 不可识别。
  • 样本太小：随机装置加入的方差使估计非常不稳定，甚至可能产生超出 \([0,1]\) 的未经约束估计。
  • 目标是判断个体行为：RRS 有意保护个体状态，只适合群体 prevalence。
  • 被试不理解或不遵守随机化说明：已知的反应机制被破坏，估计可能偏差。

docs.title: Psychometrics and R Shiny Notes
docs.text:
This site collects notes on psychometrics, Classical Test Theory (CTT), Item Response Theory (IRT), local-dependence modeling, Computerized Adaptive Testing (CAT), Cognitive Diagnosis Models (CDMs), and introductory R Shiny practice.

The material is organized by topic for course review, quick reference, and continued revision. The site is built with MkDocs + Material and supports mathematical notation, code blocks, full-text search, and structured navigation.

docs.title: Notation example
docs.text:
A common form of the two-parameter logistic model (2PL) is:

\[ P(X_{ij}=1 \mid \theta_j) = \frac{1}{1+\exp[-a_i(\theta_j-b_i)]} \]

Here, \(\theta_j\) denotes participant \(j\)'s latent trait level, \(a_i\) is the discrimination parameter of item \(i\), and \(b_i\) is its difficulty parameter.

docs.title: Evaluate the fit of the IRT model
0. Introduction: The importance of model fit
docs.text:
As with any model-based approach to psychological data interpretation, the benefits of an IRT model (e.g., item-independent examinee trait level estimates, test information curves) are achieved in direct proportion to the degree to which the data are consistent with the assumptions underlying their application.

Core content of this chapter

  1. IRT model assumptions: Assessment methods of unidimensionality and local independence
  2. Goodness of fit evaluation: Fit test at item, personnel and model levels
  3. Practical Suggestions: Additional issues to consider when applying IRT models

key challenges

The topic of model fit is an active area of current research, and to date, no clear answers exist in this area.

docs.title: 1.1 Two main assumptions
docs.text: The most commonly used IRT models make relatively simple but powerful assumptions about the relationship between item responses and latent traits:

docs.title: 1.1.1 unidimensionality assumption
docs.text:
"Appropriate" dimensionality. In the vast majority of applications, IRT models assume unidimensionality:

  • A single latent trait variable is sufficient to explain the common variance between item responses
  • Test scores (i.e., trait level estimates) are clear indicators of a single construct

docs.title: 1.1.2 local independence assumption
docs.text:
Consistent with the first assumption is the concept of local statistical independence:

  • Test items are uncorrelated (i.e. independent) while controlling for examinee trait levels
  • The probability of identifying with an item is strictly determined by the examinee’s trait level
  • is not affected by its responses to other test items or common sources of variance that are not taken into account

Relationship with CTT

The local independence assumption is similar to the assumption in CTT regarding the independent error condition based on the examinee's true score.

docs.title: 1.2 Relationship between hypotheses
docs.text:
Although conceptually different, unidimensionality and local independence are related:

  • By definition, a data set is unidimensional when item responses are locally independent based on a single latent trait.
  • See McDonald (1981) for an extended description

docs.title: 2.1 Method Overview
docs.text:
Although the development of multidimensional IRT modeling continues (e.g., Ackerman, 1994; Reckase, 1997), most commonly used IRT models assume that a single latent trait dimension governs the probability of item responses.

key questions

Even in the application of multidimensional IRT models, the correct number of latent factors must be determined a priori.

Therefore, determining the number of dimensions is a key issue in IRT modeling, regardless of whether a single-dimensional or multidimensional model is considered.

docs.title: 2.2 Traditional methods and their problems
docs.text: Hattie (1984; 1985) reviewed dozens of suggested methods for assessing matrix dimensionality:

docs.title: 2.2.1 Methods based on different principles
docs.text:
• Answer pattern consistency: e.g. Guttman scalability
  • Test-Retest Reliability
  • Principal Component Analysis: The number of eigenvalues is greater than 1.0 or the ratio of the first to the second eigenvalue
  • Factor Analysis: Output of linear and non-linear factor analysis
  • model fit statistics: Residual analysis after fitting a specific model

docs.title: 2.2.2 Problems with traditional methods
docs.text:
Hattie found that most dimensional assessment methods have serious flaws:

  1. Unable to reliably distinguish between one- and two-dimensional data sets
  2. There is no known sampling distribution
  3. Their performance under various test conditions is unknown
  4. Few guidelines exist to guide researchers

docs.title: 2.3 Active discovery
docs.text:
Although the tone was mostly negative, there were some positive findings revealed in the Hattie study:

  • Recommend using Nonlinear Factor Analysis as a possible dimensionality assessment tool
  • Especially residual variance term analysis (using programs such as NOHARM)
  • Hambleton and Rovinelli (1986) also reported that nonlinear factor analysis is promising for assessing dimensionality

docs.title: 3.1.1 Two model types
docs.text:
McDonald and Mok note that two general types of models may be suitable for item response data:

  • Complete Information Model
  • Bivariate Information Model

These provide researchers with methods to assess dimensionality and evaluate the goodness of fit of unidimensional and multidimensional IRT models.

docs.title: 3.1.2 Two forms of local independence
docs.text:
Strong form:

\[ P\{\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}|\mathbf{\theta}\} = \prod_{i=1}^{I} P_i\{X_i = x_i|\mathbf{\theta}\} \]

This equation shows that, given the latent trait vector, the probability of a joint response pattern can be decomposed into the product of the conditional probabilities of each item.

Weak form:

\[ \text{Cov}\{X_i, X_j|\mathbf{\theta}\} = 0 \]

Represents items that share variance and no longer share variance once the latent trait is taken into account.

The difference between the two forms

The weak form allows higher-order dependencies between items, while the strong form does not.

docs.title: 3.2 The concept of basic unidimensionality
docs.text: The studies of Stout (1987; 1990) and Nandakumar and Stout (1993) represent methods for assessing "basic unidimensionality".

docs.title: 3.2.1 Definition of basic unidimensionality
docs.text: A test is said to be essentially unidimensional when the average inter-item residual covariance after fitting a one-factor model approaches zero (increasing with test length).

docs.title: 3.2.2 Characteristics of the Stout program
docs.text:
• Used to identify the number of "major" common dimensions in a quiz
  • Ignore minor factors
  • No need to estimate any IRT model parameters

docs.title: 3.3 Software implementation
docs.text:
• TESTFACT（Wilson, Wood, & Gibbons, 1991）
  • NOHARM（Fraser, 1988）
  • LISCOMP（Muthén, 1987）
  • DIMTEST（Stout, 1987）

docs.title: 3.4 Suggestions
docs.text:
current situation

Researchers currently know more about what not to do than what to do when it comes to test dimensionality.

Don’ts:

  • Rely only on internal consistency indices (e.g., coefficient alpha). Alpha is affected by the number of items and average correlation, and cannot prove unidimensionality alone.
  • Use any index based on compositional analysis

Promising Directions:

  • Development of statistical fit tests and dimensionality goodness of fit indices
  • Use the new technology described previously

Key points to remember

  1. All models are strictly wrong and only approximations of reality
  2. The impact of small deviations from unidimensionality on parameter estimates remains unproven
  3. Some studies show that IRT model parameter estimates are robust to minor violations of unidimensionality

docs.title: 4.1 Definition of local dependency (LD)
docs.text:
Violations of local independence, called local dependence (LD), occur when:

  • participantitem responses not only depend on their trait level
  • Also depends on their reactions to other quiz items (or combinations of items)
  • or other common factors

docs.title: 4.2 Consequences of LD
docs.text: The existence of LD may have serious consequences on the applicability of single-dimensional IRT models:

docs.title: 4.2.1 Impact on likelihood calculation
docs.text:
The key equation for calculating participant answer pattern likelihood:

\[ L(\mathbf{x}_i|\theta_i) = \prod_{j=1}^{I} P_j(\theta_i)^{x_{ij}} \left[1-P_j(\theta_i)\right]^{1-x_{ij}} \]

Among them:

  • \(L(\mathbf{x}_i|\theta_i)\) represents the conditional probability of the item reaction mode \(\mathbf{x}_i\) of participant \(i\)
  • \(P_j(\theta_i)\) is the model probability that a participant with ability \(\theta_i\) answers correctly or agrees with item \(j\)

key questions

In order for this product form to be valid, the local independence condition must be met. When LD occurs, the product likelihood will underestimate the uncertainty caused by the correlation between items, thereby affecting parameters, information functions and ability estimates.

docs.title: 4.2.2 Empirical research findings
docs.text:
Yen (1993) demonstrated the impact of the presence of LD:

  • Quiz information is overrated
  • itemdiscrimination parameter is overestimated
  • Dimensions of latent traits that may cause IRT computer programs to identify errors (Steinberg & Thissen, 1996)

docs.title: 4.3.1 Factors in Educational Assessment
docs.text:
• Reading Comprehension Questions: Multiple questions embedded in the context of a single segment
  • Accelerated Test: Time pressure affects the response of subsequent items
  • Material Exposure Difference: There are differences between students in practice or material exposure
  • item link: Answering one item affects answers to other items

docs.title: 4.3.2 Factors in Personality Assessment
docs.text:
Steinberg and Thissen (1996) demonstrated that LD can also occur in personality assessment situations:

  • Approximately copy item: scale contains similar items
  • Response Consistency Change: participant responses become more consistent as the test progresses
  • People clarify their self-concept during testing (Knowles, 1988)

docs.title: 4.4.1 Q3 Statistics (Yen, 1984)
docs.text:
The Q3 index represents the correlation between item pairs after excluding latent trait variables.

Calculation steps:

  1. Estimate item parameters and participant trait levels
  2. Calculate each participant’s expected response to each test item
  3. Calculate residuals: observed response - expected response
  4. Residual score of associated item pairs

Explanation:

  • Since the residuals use the same ability estimate, the average value of Q3 usually has a slight negative skew. The commonly used empirical baseline is about \(-1/(I-1)\), where \(I\) is the number of items.
  • In practice, it is more common to compare the difference between the item pair Q3 and the average value of all item pairs Q3
  • Significantly larger positive values indicate possible LD

docs.title: 4.4.2 G² Statistics (Chen & Thissen, 1997)
docs.text:
\(G^2\) statistic developed to identify local dependencies:

  • Provide methods for formal analysis of residuals
  • Evaluate item pairs
  • Find unexpected covariance of other item covariance in a given quiz

docs.title: 4.5 Suggestions
docs.text:
Strategies for handling local dependencies

  1. Prevention First: Yen (1993) provides suggestions on how to arrange testing situations to minimize the chance of LD occurrence.
  2. Use quizzes: Merge items showing LD into "quizzes" (Wainer & Kiely, 1987)
  3. Note on limitations: It is difficult to form quizzes when items are not binary.

docs.title: 5.1.1 Graphical method
docs.text:
Compare estimated IRC to "empirical" IRC:

Steps to Create an Experience IRC:

  1. Estimating the parameters of the IRT model
  2. Estimating participant trait levels based on item parameters
  3. Sort and group by trait level (for example, 10 groups)
  4. Calculate the actual percentage of item recognition in each group
  5. Plot using the within-group mean trait level as a coordinate

Identify possible causes of the problem:

  • multidimensionality is not considered
  • Failure to estimate sufficient item parameters
  • Non-monotonicity of item-trait relationship
  • participant samples come from different groups
  • poorly constructed item

docs.title: 5.1.2 Statistical methods
docs.text:
Bock (1972) Chi-Square Index:

\[ \text{BCHI} = \sum_{g=1}^{G} \frac{N_g(O_{ig} - E_{ig})^2}{E_{ig}(1-E_{ig})} \]

Among them:

  • \(O_{ig}\) is the observed correct proportion of item \(i\) in the interval \(g\)
  • \(E_{ig}\) is the expected correct proportion based on the interval median trait level
  • \(N_g\) is the number of participants in the interval \(g\)

Degrees of freedom: \(G - m\) (\(m\) is the estimated number of item parameters)

Things to note

Like many chi-square statistics, these fit tests are very sensitive to sample size and probably should not be considered reliable decision-making tools.

BILOG Likelihood Ratio Chi-Square:

\[ \chi^2 = 2\sum\left[R_g \log\frac{R_g}{N_g P(\theta_M)} + (N_g - R_g)\log\frac{N_g - R_g}{N_g(1-P(\theta_M))}\right] \]
  • Degrees of freedom equal to the number of θ groups
  • Theta groups are collapsed to avoid expectation less than 2

docs.title: 5.1.3 Standardized residuals
docs.text:
For Rasch models, standardized residuals can be calculated:

Expected reaction:

\[ E[x_{si}] = \sum_{k=0}^{K-1} kP_i(\theta_s) \]

variance:

\[ V[x_{si}] = \sum_{k=0}^{K-1}(k-E[x_{si}])^2 P_i(\theta_s) \]

Standardized Residuals:

\[ z_{si} = \frac{x_{si} - E[x_{si}]}{\sqrt{V[x_{si}]}} \]

Fit Statistics:

  • item fitting: \(\text{Item fit} = \sum \frac{z_{si}^2}{N}\)
  • Personnel fitting: \(\text{Person fit} = \sum \frac{z_{si}^2}{I}\)

docs.title: 5.2.1 Purpose of Personnel Fit Index
docs.text:
• Evaluate IRTmodel fit at the individual level
  • Evaluate effectiveness of participant
  • Evaluate the validity and meaningfulness of test scores

docs.title: 5.2.2 Types of Personnel Fit Index
docs.text:
• Appropriateness Measure (Levine & Rubin, 1979)
  • caution index (Tatsuoka, 1984; 1996)
  • Scalability Index (Reise & Waller, 1993)

docs.title: 5.2.3 ZL Statistics (Drasgow, Levine & Williams, 1985)
docs.text:
Log-likelihood:

\[ \text{LogL}|\theta_s = [x_{si} \times \log(P_i|\theta_s)] + [(1-x_{si}) \times \log(1-P_i|\theta_s)] \]

expectation:

\[ E[\text{LogL}|\theta_s] = \sum\{P_i|\theta_s \times \log(P_i|\theta_s) + Q_i|\theta_s \times \log(Q_i|\theta_s)\} \]

variance:

\[ V(\text{LogL}|\theta_s) = \sum\{P_i|\theta_s)(Q_i|\theta_s)[\log(P_i|\theta_s)/Q_i|\theta_s)]^2 \]

Normalized \(Z_L\) Index:

\[ Z_L|\theta_s = \frac{\sum[\text{LogL}|\theta_s - \sum E(\text{LogL}|\theta_s)]}{(\sum V(\text{LogL}|\theta_s))^{1/2}} \]

  • The conditional null distribution of \(Z_L\) is standard normal
  • Large negative \(Z_L\) values (for example, < -2.0) indicate a poor fit
  • Large positive \(Z_L\) values indicate a more likely response pattern than predicted by the model

docs.title: 5.2.4 Application of Personnel Fitting
docs.text:
• Identify Abnormal Test Behavior: Cheating, groping, careless or inconsistent responses
  • Data Cleaning: Identify abnormal participants
  • Personality Assessment: Identify structural differences in individual personality traits
  • Diagnostic Use: Identify specific skill deficits or cognitive errors

docs.title: 5.2.5 Issues in Personnel Fitting Research
docs.text:
1. Explanation Difficulties: Unable to explain the reasons for non-fitting
  2. Sampling distribution: The actual null distribution may not be as good as theoretical expectations
  3. statistical power: limited ability to identify response bias

Improve conditions for statistical power

  • Longer quizzes (e.g., more than 30 items)
  • Extensive range of itemdifficulty parameters
  • Highly differentiated test items

docs.title: 5.3.1 Nested model comparison (Thissen, 1986)
docs.text:
By comparing the log-likelihoods of different models:

Example: Comparing 2PL and 1PL models

  1. Estimate the 2PL model and calculate the log likelihood
  2. Apply constraints (all slopes are equal) and estimate the 1PL model
  3. Compare the difference in log-likelihood of two models
  4. The difference distribution is chi-square, degrees of freedom = number of parameter differences

Limit

  • Under sparse contingency table conditions, the distribution of changes in \(G^2\) may not be chi-squared
  • More research is needed to confirm

docs.title: 5.3.2 Ideal Observer Method (Maydeu-Olivares, Drasgow & Mead, 1994)
docs.text:
• Can compare non-nested models
  • Based on the likelihood of observing item response patterns under various models
  • When the likelihood is approximately equal across models, there is no difference in which model is ultimately chosen

docs.title: 6.1.1 The Importance of Conceptual Model
docs.text:
First assess the measured construct and the conceptual model underlying the construct:

Manifest variables vs latent variables:

  • Manifest variable: defined by its indicators (e.g. economic strength, health)
  • Latent variables: Cause indicators to be related (such as intelligence, extraversion)

Key differences

IRT models are "latent" variable models, assuming causal relationships from latent traits to indicators. If you simply apply the IRT model to manifest variables, it will inevitably lead to problems.

docs.title: 6.1.2 Good exploration of model fit
docs.text:
Good model fit exploration should include:

  1. Dimensionality Assessment: Use DIMTEST or nonlinear factor analysis
  2. local independence test: Q3 or G² statistics
  3. Residual analysis: Check the residual covariance term
  4. item fitting: graphical and statistical methods
  5. Personnel Fitting: Identifying Abnormal Response Patterns

docs.title: 6.2 Perspectives on model selection
docs.text:
Prudence

We take a more cautious approach to model selection for the following reasons:

Model choice is usually obvious:

  • Two-category item + guess → 3PL model
  • Personality assessment data → 2PL model

Actual impact may be limited:

  • For research applications, as long as the data has strong one-dimensionality and the sample size is large enough
  • It may not make much difference which specific IRT model is actually adopted

need attention

Goldstein (1980) noted that different models can have significant effects on the relative scales at which individuals are mapped onto the latent trait continuum.

docs.title: 6.3 Summary
docs.text:
This chapter introduces methods for evaluating IRTmodel fit:

  1. Evaluation of Model Assumptions is the basis
  2. Multi-level fit assessment is necessary
  3. New methods are constantly evolving
  4. Practical application requires comprehensive judgment

Remember: all models are wrong, but some are useful. The key is to ensure that violations of the model's assumptions do not significantly affect the study's conclusions.

The content of this chapter is based on Chapter 9 of Embretson & Reise (2000)

docs.title: Classic Measurement Theory (CTT) and Item Response Theory (IRT)
0.1 Development of Classical Measurement Theory (CTT)
docs.text:
Historical context

  • 1907-1913: Spearman laid the foundation for classical measurement theory
  • 1950: Gulliksen publishes classic textbooks, and the CTT system matures
  • 1968: Lord and Novick proposed Item Response Theory (IRT)
  • Now: IRT is becoming more mainstream, but CTT is still widely used

docs.title: 0.2.1 What is "equating" (Equating)?
docs.text:
Definition and application of equating

equating: The process of making different versions of a test comparable

Actual example:

  • There are multiple sets of test papers for the college entrance examination, but the final scores must be comparable to each other.
  • SAT has new items every year, but the score standards must remain the same.
  • Each person’s items in the computer-based TOEFL test are different, but the scores must be fair.

Traditional equating method:

  1. Linear equating: \(Y = aX + b\) (simple linear transformation)
  2. Nonlinear equating: Use more complex curve relationships

**Why is nonlinear equating needed? **

Because the score distribution of different tests may be different:

  • Test A: Most people get average scores, showing normal distribution
  • Quiz B: Many people get high or low scores, the distribution is skewed
  • Simple linear transformation cannot handle this difference

docs.title: 0.2.2 What is the "Delta method"?
docs.text:
Detailed explanation of Delta method

Delta method: item difficulty indicator proposed by Gulliksen (1950)

Core formula:

\[\Delta = 13 + 4\Phi^{-1}(p)\]

Among them:

  • \(p\) = item pass rate (proportion of people who answered correctly)
  • \(\Phi^{-1}\) = inverse function of standard normal distribution
  • 13 and 4 are to avoid negative numbers and decimals

Intuitive understanding:

  • If 50% of people answer correctly, \(p=0.5\), \(\Delta = 13\) (medium difficulty)
  • If 90% of people answer correctly, \(p=0.9\) and \(\Delta\) are smaller (simple item)
  • If 10% of people answer correctly, \(p=0.1\), \(\Delta\) is larger (difficult item)

docs.title: 0.2.3 What is "interval scale"?
docs.text:
Four levels of measurement scale:

  1. Nominal scale: can only be classified (eg: male/female)
  2. Sequential scale: Can be sorted but with unequal spacing (such as: satisfactory/average/unsatisfactory)
  3. Interval scale: equal intervals but no absolute zero (such as temperature)
  4. Ratio scale: There is an absolute zero point (such as: height, weight)

Characteristics of interval scale

  • Differences between values are meaningful
  • The difference between 60 points and 70 points = The difference between 70 points and 80 points
  • But you can't say that 80 points is "twice as good" as 40 points

Questions in psychometrics: The raw score number usually does not meet the requirements of interval scale and needs to be achieved through statistical transformation.

docs.title: 0.2.4 What is "norm"?
docs.text:
Norm

Definition: Performance standards of a reference group

Example:

  • A student scored 100 points on the IQ test
  • The score itself is meaningless
  • But if the norm shows: mean score = 100, standard deviation = 15
  • Then this student is "average"

Common norm scores:

  • Percentile: what percentage of people exceed
  • Standard score: \((X-\mu)/\sigma\)
  • T Score: \(50 + 10 \times \text{standard score}\)

docs.title: 0.2.5 What is "difficulty parallelism"?
docs.text:
Difficulty Parallel Concepts and Issues

Difficulty parallelism: The overall difficulty of different test versions is the same

Traditional Practice:

  • Each version contains the same proportion of easy, medium and difficult items
  • Same average difficulty
  • Score distribution is similar

Question: This approach assumes that everyone has the same ability distribution, which is often not the case.

docs.title: 0.2.6 What is "question stimulation"?
docs.text:
The influence of question stem stimulation

Question stimulus: non-core factors in the item that affect the answer

Example: Math question: "Xiao Ming bought 3 apples..."

  • Core: Test computing power
  • Stimulus: person’s name (Xiao Ming), object (apple), situation (shopping)

Comparison of views:

  • Conventional View: These stimuli do not affect the measurement
  • Modern Perspective: Stimuli may affect performance in different groups
  • Urban children are familiar with the situation of "buying apples"
  • Rural children may be more familiar with the situation of "growing apples"

docs.title: 0.2.7 What is "Score Interpretation"?
docs.text:
Scores explained: How to understand and use quiz scores

  1. Absolute interpretation: The fraction itself has a fixed meaning
  2. Example: The passing mark for the exam is 60 points
  3. Relative Interpretation: The performance of scores relative to others
  4. Example: Top 10%
  5. Intra-individual interpretation: Comparison of the same person at different times
  6. Example: This time it is 5 points better than last time

docs.title: 1. CTT basic theory and formula derivation
1.1 Basic assumptions and derivation of CTT
1.1.1 Origin of core formula
docs.text:
Basic assumptions of CTT

Basic formula:

\[X = T + E\]

Among them:

  • \(X\) = observed score (actually measured score)
  • \(T\) = true fraction (theoretical "real" fraction)
  • \(E\) = Measurement error (random fluctuation)

Further assumptions:

  1. \(E(E) = 0\) (error expectation is 0)
  2. \(\rho(T,E) = 0\) (the true fraction is not related to the error)
  3. \(\rho(E_1,E_2) = 0\) (errors in different measurements are not relevant)

docs.title: 1.1.2 Derivation of reliability formula
docs.text:
Step 1: Decompose the variance of the observed scores

\[\text{Var}(X) = \text{Var}(T + E) = \text{Var}(T) + \text{Var}(E) + 2\text{Cov}(T,E)\]

Due to \(\text{Cov}(T,E) = 0\):

\[\sigma_X^2 = \sigma_T^2 + \sigma_E^2\]

Step 2: Define reliability

Reliability is the proportion of true fractional variance to total variance:

\[r_{tt} = \frac{\sigma_T^2}{\sigma_X^2} = \frac{\sigma_T^2}{\sigma_T^2 + \sigma_E^2}\]

Step 3: Derive the standard error formula

Available from \(\sigma_X^2 = \sigma_T^2 + \sigma_E^2\):

\[\sigma_E^2 = \sigma_X^2 - \sigma_T^2 = \sigma_X^2(1 - \frac{\sigma_T^2}{\sigma_X^2}) = \sigma_X^2(1 - r_{tt})\]

Therefore:

\[SE_{\text{msmt}} = \sigma_E = \sigma_X\sqrt{1 - r_{tt}}\]

CTT standard error formula summary

standard error formula:

\[SE_{\text{msmt}} = \sigma \sqrt{1 - r_{tt}}\]

Derivation logic:

  1. Observed fraction = true fraction + error
  2. Total variance = true fraction variance + error variance
  3. reliability = true fraction variance / total variance
  4. standard error = standard deviation of error

docs.title: 1.2.1 Question setting
docs.text: Suppose we have a test with a reliability of \(r_{tt}\). Now we want to know: if the test length is increased to \(n\) times, what will the new reliability be?

docs.title: 1.2.2 Detailed derivation process
docs.text:
Step 1: Set variables

  • Original test: length is \(k\), reliability is \(r_{tt}\)
  • New test: length \(nk\), reliability \(r_{nn}\) (to be requested)

Step 2: Analyze variance changes

Variance breakdown of the original test:

\[\sigma_X^2 = \sigma_T^2 + \sigma_E^2\]

When the test length increases by \(n\) times:

  • The true fraction variance increases by \(n^2\) times: \(\sigma_{T_n}^2 = n^2\sigma_T^2\)
  • The error variance increases by \(n\) times: \(\sigma_{E_n}^2 = n\sigma_E^2\) (assuming the errors are independent)

Step 3: Calculate the new total variance

\[\sigma_{X_n}^2 = \sigma_{T_n}^2 + \sigma_{E_n}^2 = n^2\sigma_T^2 + n\sigma_E^2\]

Step 4: Calculate new reliability

\[r_{nn} = \frac{\sigma_{T_n}^2}{\sigma_{X_n}^2} = \frac{n^2\sigma_T^2}{n^2\sigma_T^2 + n\sigma_E^2} = \frac{n^2\sigma_T^2}{n(n\sigma_T^2 + \sigma_E^2)}\]

Simplify:

\[r_{nn} = \frac{n\sigma_T^2}{n\sigma_T^2 + \sigma_E^2}\]

Step 5: Use original reliability expression

Available from \(r_{tt} = \frac{\sigma_T^2}{\sigma_T^2 + \sigma_E^2}\):

  • \(\sigma_T^2 = r_{tt}(\sigma_T^2 + \sigma_E^2)\)
  • \(\sigma_E^2 = (1-r_{tt})(\sigma_T^2 + \sigma_E^2)\)

Assume \(\sigma_T^2 + \sigma_E^2 = V\), then:

\[r_{nn} = \frac{n \cdot r_{tt} \cdot V}{n \cdot r_{tt} \cdot V + (1-r_{tt}) \cdot V} = \frac{nr_{tt}}{nr_{tt} + (1-r_{tt})}\]

Spearman-Brown formula

Final formula:

\[r_{nn} = \frac{nr_{tt}}{1 + (n-1)r_{tt}}\]

Special circumstances:

  • \(n=2\) (double the length): \(r_{22} = \frac{2r_{tt}}{1 + r_{tt}}\)
  • \(n=0.5\) (halved length): \(r_{0.5} = \frac{0.5r_{tt}}{1 - 0.5r_{tt}}\)

docs.title: 1.2.3 Numerical examples
docs.text:
Assume the original test reliability \(r_{tt} = 0.6\):

Double the length (\(n=2\)):

\[r_{22} = \frac{2 \times 0.6}{1 + (2-1) \times 0.6} = \frac{1.2}{1.6} = 0.75\]

Length increased by 3 times (\(n=3\)):

\[r_{33} = \frac{3 \times 0.6}{1 + (3-1) \times 0.6} = \frac{1.8}{2.2} = 0.82\]

Length halved (\(n=0.5\)):

\[r_{0.5} = \frac{0.5 \times 0.6}{1 + (0.5-1) \times 0.6} = \frac{0.3}{0.7} = 0.43\]

docs.title: 2.1 The core idea of IRT
docs.text:
A revolutionary perspective on IRT

  1. Individual differences: People with different ability levels have different measurement accuracy.
  2. item features: Each question has its own difficulty and distinction.
  3. Model driven: based on probabilistic models rather than simple statistics
  4. Invariance: item parameters do not depend on specific samples

docs.title: 2.2 The simplest IRT model: Rasch model
2.2.1 Model formula
docs.text:
\[P_i(\theta) = \frac{e^{(\theta - b_i)}}{1 + e^{(\theta - b_i)}}\]

Among them:

  • \(P_i(\theta)\) = The probability that a person with ability \(\theta\) correctly answers question \(i\)
  • \(\theta\) = Human ability parameter (trait level)
  • \(b_i\) = difficulty parameter of question \(i\)
  • \(e\) = natural constant

docs.title: 2.2.2 Model features
docs.text:
When \(\theta = b_i\):

\[P_i(\theta) = \frac{e^0}{1 + e^0} = \frac{1}{2} = 0.5\]

This means: when the person's ability is equal to the item difficulty, the probability of getting the answer right is 50%.

When \(\theta >> b_i\):

\[P_i(\theta) \approx 1\]

(Ability is much higher than difficulty, the answer is almost certain to be correct)

When \(\theta << b_i\):

\[P_i(\theta) \approx 0\]

(The ability is far lower than the difficulty level, and the answer is almost certainly wrong)

Updated June 2025

docs.title: item parameters estimation: calibration of IRT model
0. Introduction: The core issue of item parameters estimation
0.1 Chapter Positioning and Premise
docs.text:
In Chapter 7, we learned how to estimate the examinee's ability level, but that time assumed that the item parameters were known. In reality, when developing a new test, item parameters must first be estimated. This is the central question to be addressed in this chapter.

fundamental challenge

To estimate item difficulty, you need to know the student's ability; to estimate the student's ability, you need to know the item difficulty.

How to start when neither is known?

docs.title: 0.2 Data used in this chapter
docs.text:
All methods in this chapter will be demonstrated on the 10-item data of the Abstract Reasoning Test (ART):

  • sample size: 818 young adults (787 valid samples, excluding 31 extreme scores)
  • Number of items: 10, choose 1 from 8 (the probability of guessing is extremely small)
  • model fit: reasonably fit the Rasch model

docs.title: 0.3 Prerequisite assumptions for estimation
docs.text:
Two key assumptions

  1. local independence: After controlling the ability, the responses of each item are independent of each other.
  2. unidimensionality: The test measures a single latent trait

For ART data, the correlation between items is overall significant (χ²₄₅ = 550.154, p < .000), but the residual correlation is not significant after controlling for single factor (χ²₃₅ = 41.980, p = .194), supporting the local independence hypothesis.

docs.title: 1.1.1 Method principle
docs.text:
Rasch (1960) showed how to estimate item parameters by hand calculation from the basic data matrix. The key idea is:

  • The rows represent items and the columns represent people with equal abilities (grouped by total score)
  • total score is a sufficient statistic for estimating ability
  • The number of people passing an item is a sufficient statistic for estimating difficulty.

docs.title: 1.1.2 Construct basic data matrix
docs.text:

  • Within the same row, the passing rate increases as ability increases
  • Within the same column, the pass rate decreases with item difficulty

docs.title: 1.1.3 Logarithmic ratio conversion
docs.text:
To obtain estimates consistent with the Rasch model, the pass rates need to be converted to log ratios:

\[ \log \text{odds}_{ig} = \log_e\left(\frac{P_{ig}}{1-P_{ig}}\right) \]

For example, the logarithmic ratio of item7 in score group 5:

\[ \log \text{odds}_{75} = \log_e\left(\frac{0.89}{0.11}\right) = 2.09 \]

item 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 mean Rasch difficulty 7 -.45 -.27 .78 1.48 2.09 1.83 2.77 3.89 Big 1.86 -1.91 10 -1.27 .28 .50 1.10 1.79 2.31 2.31 3.56 3.18 1.52 -1.57 ... ... ... ... ... ... ... ... ... ... ... ... Ability θ -2.68 -1.61 -.98 -.73 -.45 -.19 .08 .53 1.18

(Note: "Large" in the table means maximum value, and continuity correction is used in actual calculations)

docs.title: 1.1.4 Parameter estimation
docs.text:
1. Calculate the average log ratio of each row (item)
  2. Calculate the overall item mean: -0.05
  3. item difficulty = -(row mean - overall mean)

For example, item7:

  • row mean = 1.86
  • bias = 1.86 - (-0.05) = 1.91
  • Difficulty = -1.91 (easy items have negative difficulty values)

docs.title: 1.1.5 Realization of group invariance
docs.text:
Why is it not affected by the sample distribution?

The key is unweighted averaging: each ability group is equally weighted, regardless of how many people are in the group.

This ensures that the item parameter estimates remain the same regardless of whether more good students or more poor students are tested.

docs.title: 1.2 Logistic regression method with known ability
docs.text: Assuming that the abilities of the 787 participants are known (actually estimated using MML), logistic regression can be used to estimate the item parameters.

docs.title: 1.2.1 Model Settings
docs.text:
Logistic regression model:

\[ P(x_i = 1) = \frac{\exp(y)}{1 + \exp(y)} \]

Among them \(y = b_0 + b_1\theta\)

For 2PL model, reparameterize: \(y = \alpha_i(\theta - \beta_i)\)

Therefore:

  • Discrimination: \(\alpha_i = b_1\)
  • Difficulty: \(\beta_i = -b_0/b_1\)

docs.title: 1.2.2 Estimated result comparison
docs.text:
Table 8.4 Heuristic item estimation

item library P value basic data matrix Logistic regression 7 .84 -1.91 -1.65 10 .82 -1.57 -1.50 13 .65 -.68 -.50 8 .66 -.46 -.45 27 .60 -.09 -.17 19 .47 .25 .46 16 .45 .54 .55 33 .40 1.01 .90 22 .38 1.06 .91 28 .26 1.87 1.57

Estimates from the two methods are highly consistent (r² = .99).

docs.title: 2.1.1 Likelihood of a single reaction
docs.text:
For a bipartite reaction (x ∈ {0,1}), the likelihood is:

\[ P(X_{is}) = P_i^{X_{is}} Q_i^{1-X_{is}} \]

Among them \(Q_i = 1 - P_i\)

docs.title: 2.1.2 Likelihood of complete data
docs.text:
Assuming local independence, the data likelihood is:

\[ L(\mathbf{X}) = \prod_s \prod_i P_{is}^{X_{is}} Q_{is}^{1-X_{is}} \]

Log likelihood:

\[ \ln L(\mathbf{X}) = \sum_s \sum_i [X_{is} \ln P_{is} + (1-X_{is}) \ln Q_{is}] \]

docs.title: 2.2 Search process
docs.text:
The likelihood function is in an inverted U shape and has a unique maximum value.

The estimating equation (first derivative) is zero at the maximum value.

docs.title: 2.3 Newton-Raphson method
docs.text:
Iteration formula:

\[ \beta_{\text{improved}} = \beta_{\text{current}} - \frac{L'(\beta_{\text{current}})}{L''(\beta_{\text{current}})} \]

Among them:

  • \(L'\): First derivative (estimate equation)
  • \(L''\): Second derivative (curvature information)

docs.title: 2.4 standard error calculation
docs.text:
For the Rasch model:

\[ SE(\beta) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\sum_s P_{is}(1-P_{is})}} \]

When \(P_{is} = 0.5\), the standard error is the smallest.

docs.title: 3. Three ways to deal with unknown abilities
3.1.1 Basic idea
docs.text:
Alternate estimates:

  1. Fixed item parameters and estimated capabilities
  2. Fixed capabilities, estimate item parameters
  3. Repeat until convergence

docs.title: 3.1.2 Estimation equation
docs.text:
For the Rasch model:

\[ \sum_s X_{is} = \sum_s P(X_{is} = 1|\theta_s, \beta_i) \]

The left side is the observed correct number, and the right side is the expected correct number predicted by the model.

docs.title: 3.1.3 Problems with JML
docs.text:
• Parameter estimates are biased
  • Inconsistency (increasing samples does not improve accuracy)
  • Cannot handle extreme scores

docs.title: 3.2.1 Core idea
docs.text:
Treat abilities as random variables and eliminate them by integration:

\[ P(\mathbf{X}_r|\mathbf{\beta}) = \int P(\mathbf{X}_r|\theta, \mathbf{\beta}) g(\theta) d\theta \]

where \(g(\theta)\) is the capability distribution (usually assumed to be standard normal).

docs.title: 3.2.2 Numerical integration
docs.text:
Use the Gaussian quadrature approximation:

\[ P(\mathbf{X}_r|\mathbf{\beta}) \approx \sum_{q=1}^Q P(\mathbf{X}_r|\theta_q, \mathbf{\beta}) w_q \]

docs.title: 3.2.3 EM algorithm
docs.text:
Step E: Calculate expected frequency

  • Expected number of people at ability point \(\theta_q\): \(N'_q\)
  • The expected number of people who answered item \(i\) correctly in \(\theta_q\): \(R_{iq}\)

M-step: Maximize expected log-likelihood

\[ \sum_q R_{iq} = \sum_q N'_q P_i(\theta_q, \beta_i) \]

docs.title: 3.3.1 sufficient statistics
docs.text: In the Rasch model, the total score \(r\) is the sufficient statistic of ability.

docs.title: 3.3.2 Conditional probability
docs.text:
Given the total score, the probability of the reaction pattern:

\[ P(\mathbf{X}|r, \mathbf{\beta}) = \frac{\prod_i e^{-\beta_i X_i}}{\gamma_r} \]

Note: ability parameter \(\theta\) has completely disappeared!

docs.title: 3.3.3 Basic symmetry functions
docs.text:
\(\gamma_r\) is a basic symmetry function of order \(r\), representing all possible ways to get \(r\) points.

For example, a 4-question quiz:

  • \(\gamma_0 = 1\)
  • \(\gamma_1 = e^{-\beta_1} + e^{-\beta_2} + e^{-\beta_3} + e^{-\beta_4}\)
  • \(\gamma_2 = e^{-\beta_1-\beta_2} + e^{-\beta_1-\beta_3} + ...\) (6 items)
  • \(\gamma_3 = e^{-\beta_1-\beta_2-\beta_3} + ...\) (4 items)
  • \(\gamma_4 = e^{-\beta_1-\beta_2-\beta_3-\beta_4}\)

docs.title: 4.1 Method selection decision
docs.text:
Practical Decision Making Guide

situation Recommended method Reason Rasch model + large sample (N≥500) CML optimal properties Rasch model + small sample (N<500) MML more stable 2PL/3PL model MML only option Need to deal with extreme scores MML JML/CML cannot be processed

docs.title: 4.2 sample size requirements
docs.text:
• Rasch model: minimum 200 people
  • 2PL model: minimum 500 people
  • 3PL model: minimum 1000 people

docs.title: 4.3 Software implementation
docs.text:
• Rasch model: Winsteps (JML/CML), ConQuest (MML)
  • 2PL/3PL model: BILOG-MG (MML), mirt package (MML)

docs.title: 5.1 Derivatives of JML
docs.text:
Table 8.6 First and second derivatives of 1PL, 2PL and 3PL IRT models

model parameters first derivative second derivative 1PL(Rasch) Difficulty \(-\sum_s (X_{is} - P_{is})\) \(-\sum_s P_{is}(1-P_{is})\) 2PL Discrimination \(\sum_s (X_{is} - P_{is})(\theta_s - \beta_i)\) \(-\sum_s P_{is}(1-P_{is})(\theta_s - \beta_i)^2\) 2PL Difficulty \(-\alpha_i \sum_s (X_{is} - P_{is})\) \(-\alpha_i^2 \sum_s P_{is}(1-P_{is})\)

docs.title: 5.2 Expected frequency of MML
docs.text:
The expected number of people who answer item \(i\) correctly at ability point \(\theta_q\):

\[ R_{iq} = \sum_p n_p x_{ip} P(\theta_q|\mathbf{X}_p, \mathbf{\beta}) \]

where the posterior probability is:

\[ P(\theta_q|\mathbf{X}_p, \mathbf{\beta}) = \frac{w_q L(\mathbf{X}_p|\theta_q, \mathbf{\beta})}{\sum_{q'} w_{q'} L(\mathbf{X}_p|\theta_{q'}, \mathbf{\beta})} \]

docs.title: 5.3 Conditional probability of CML
docs.text:
Given the total score \(r\), the probability of answering item \(i\) correctly:

\[ P(X_i = 1|r, \mathbf{\beta}) = e^{-\beta_i} \frac{\gamma_{r-1}^{(i)}}{\gamma_r} \]

Among them, \(\gamma_{r-1}^{(i)}\) is the basic symmetry function after removing item \(i\).

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
This chapter introduces methods for estimating IRTitem parameters:

  1. Heuristics provide intuitive understanding and demonstrate group invariance
  2. Maximum Likelihood Principle is the basis of modern estimation methods
  3. Three ML methods each have their own advantages and disadvantages:
  4. JML: simple but biased
  5. MML: complex but the best quality
  6. CML: elegant but only Rasch model

When choosing a method, you need to consider the model type, sample size, and actual needs. MML is the mainstream choice for modern IRT software.

The content of this chapter is based on Chapter 8 of Embretson & Reise (2000)

docs.title: 0. Why are better measurement methods needed?
docs.text:
Thinking questions

Suppose you are a teacher with two students:

  • Xiao Ming scored 80 points on a simple test paper
  • Xiaohong scored 70 points on a difficult test paper

**Question: Who has more ability? **

This seemingly simple question reveals the fundamental flaw of traditional testing theory (CTT). Today, we will learn how Item Response Theory (IRT) solves this problem.

docs.title: 1.1 Latent variable problem
docs.text:
core concepts

Latent Variables: Psychological traits that are not directly observable but affect observable behavior

Manifest Variables: Behavioral performance that can be directly observed and recorded

Let’s use an analogy with medical diagnosis:

Analog object Visible information inferred target medical diagnosis Fever 38.5°C, cough, fatigue maybe the flu psychometrics Correct answer to question 1, incorrect answer to question 5, total score 75 points What is the competency level?

Key differences

Doctors have thermometers that can accurately measure fever levels, but how do psychologists "measure" invisible abilities? That's why we need measurement models!

docs.title: 1.2 Comparison of two measurement models
docs.text:
Classical Testing Theory (CTT):

  • Follow total score
  • Model: Observed Score = True Score + Error
  • Simple but limited

Item Response Theory (IRT):

  • Pay attention to the reaction of each item
  • Model: P(correct answer) = f(ability, item parameters)
  • Complex but more precise

docs.title: 2. Three fatal flaws of CTT
docs.text:
The fundamental problem of CTT

  1. Test dependency: If you change the set of questions, the meaning of the scores will change.
  2. Information waste: only use total score and ignore the answer mode
  3. Unable to separate parameters: I don’t know whether the high score is due to strong ability or simple items

docs.title: 2.1 Case analysis: Why is CTT not enough?
docs.text:
Consider the following situation:

student Answer mode total score CTT conclusion A Answer questions 1-4 (easy questions) 4 points Same ability B Answer questions 2-5 (including difficult questions) 4 points Same ability

Are they really the same?

If question 5 is much more difficult than question 1, does student B’s correct answer to question 5 mean that he is more capable? CTT cannot answer this question!

docs.title: 3.1 Rasch model: the simplest IRT model
docs.text:
The core idea of Rasch model

The probability of correct answer depends on:

  • Ability (θ): individual’s latent trait level
  • Difficulty (β): difficulty parameter of item

When ability = difficulty, probability of correct answer = 50%

docs.title: 3.1.1 Formal expression
docs.text:
Logarithmic probability form (intuitive understanding):

\[ \ln\left[\frac{P_{\text{correct}}}{P_{\text{incorrect}}}\right] = \theta - \beta \]

Probability form (actual calculation):

\[ P(\text{correct}) = \frac{e^{(\theta - \beta)}}{1 + e^{(\theta - \beta)}} \]

memory skills

  • θ > β: ability exceeds difficulty → probability of correct answer > 50%
  • θ = β: Difficulty of ability matching → Probability of correct answer = 50%
  • θ < β: difficulty exceeds ability → probability of correct answer < 50%

docs.title: 3.2 item characteristic curve (ICC)
docs.text:
of the three items in the Rasch model

Key Features of ICC

  1. S-shaped curve: steep in the middle and gentle at both ends
  2. Position parameter: The curve moves left and right to indicate different levels of difficulty.
  3. Parallel Curves: All ICCs in the Rasch model are parallel (same slope)

docs.title: 3.3 Real data example
docs.text:
Let’s look at the data from Rasch’s original study:

Data characteristics

  1. The probability increases monotonically with the total score.
  2. Present an S-shaped growth pattern
  3. The item curves do not intersect (maintain difficulty order)

docs.title: 4.1 From summation to search
docs.text:
fundamental change

CTT method: Depends on total score total score = \(\sum\) item score ability estimate = standardized total score

IRT method: Probability-based maximum likelihood estimation

For every possible \(\theta\):

  • Calculate \(L(\text{observed response pattern} \mid \theta)\)
  • Select \(\theta\) that maximizes \(L\) as the ability estimate

docs.title: 4.2 Specific calculation examples
docs.text:
Suppose there are 5 questions, the difficulty is (-2, -1, 0, 1, 2), and a student’s answer pattern is (1,1,1,1,0):

Likelihood calculation process

Step 1: Choose a candidate θ value (e.g. θ = 0)

Step 2: Calculate the probability of correct answer for each question:

item Difficulty β Actual answer \(P(\text{correct}\mid \theta=0)\) 1 -2 Correct answer 0.88 2 -1 Correct answer 0.73 3 0 Correct answer 0.50 4 1 Correct answer 0.27 5 2 Wrong answer 0.12

Step 3: Calculate likelihood L = 0.88 × 0.73 × 0.50 × 0.27 × (1 - 0.12) = 0.076

Step 4: Try other values of θ and find the θ that maximizes L

docs.title: 4.3 Visualization of search process
docs.text:
Key findings

  • The likelihood curve shapes of different answering modes are different -The peak position is the best ability estimate
  • Inconsistent answering patterns (such as answering difficult questions correctly first and then answering easy questions incorrectly) are less likely

docs.title: 5.1 Why is discrimination parameter needed?
docs.text:
think

Are all items equally valid?

  • Some items can well differentiate students with different abilities
  • Some items have poor differentiation effect

docs.title: 5.2 2PL model formula
docs.text:
\[ P(\text{correct}) = \frac{e^{α(\theta - β)}}{1 + e^{α(\theta - β)}} \]

Among them:

  • α discrimination = parameter (slope)
  • The larger α is, the steeper the curve is and the better the discrimination effect is.

with different degrees of discrimination

important difference

In the 2PL model, the total score is no longer sufficient statistic!

Two students with the same total score, if:

  • Student A: Mainly answered items with low discrimination correctly.
  • Student B: Mainly answered items with high distinction correctly.

Then: → Student B will get a higher ability estimate

Explanation of reasons:

In 2PL, the discrimination parameter (α) of each question affects the "information content" of the answer. Highly differentiated questions contribute more to the ability estimate, so → Students with the same total score but different problem-solving modes will have different ability estimates.

In other words: The total score cannot capture "which questions were answered correctly", so it is not a sufficient statistic.

docs.title: 6.1 Test equating problem
docs.text:
IRT solutions

By including item parameters, IRT automatically adjusts for the impact of different test difficulties

Get 4 questions correct on the hard test → higher ability estimate

Get 4 questions correct on the easy test → lower ability estimate

ability estimate reliability

  • Horizontal axis θ: Which θ gives the highest probability of the response pattern predicted by the model → is the student’s ability estimate
  • Vertical axis L(θ): The height of the maximum likelihood value indicates the "reasonableness" or "internal consistency" of the reaction pattern

Example comparison:

  • Pattern 1 (1,1,1,1,0): Answer 4 questions correctly on the easy questions, θ ≈ 1, high likelihood value → stable estimation
  • Pattern 4 (1,1,1,0,1): Answer 4 questions correctly on more difficult questions, θ ≈ 2.5, the likelihood value is also higher → stronger ability
  • Pattern 2 (1,1,0,1,0): alternating right and wrong, inconsistent answers, overall likelihood value is low → ability estimate is unstable and untrustworthy

docs.title: 6.2 Adaptability Test (CAT)
docs.text:
IRT makes CAT possible

  1. Select the item with the most appropriate difficulty based on the current ability estimate
  2. Update ability estimate in real time
  3. Stop testing when the accuracy requirements are met.

result: shorter tests, more accurate measurements!

docs.title: 7. Summary: IRT vs CTT
docs.text:
IRT’s revolutionary contribution

Features CTT IRT measurement invariance ❌ Rely on specific tests ✅ Stable across tests Information Utilization ❌ Only use total score ✅ Utilize quiz mode Parameter separation ❌ Mix it up ✅ Ability and item are independent Measurement accuracy ❌ Assuming constant ✅Varies with ability Adaptability Test ❌ Not supported ✅Natural support

core concept

CTT asked: "How many points did you score?"

IRT asks: "Based on your answering pattern and item characteristics, what ability level is most likely to produce this result?"

**This is the essential leap from "scoring" to "measurement"! **

docs.title: 8. Think and practice
docs.text:
Thoughts after class

  1. Why is IRT said to be a "model-based" measurement?
  2. Under what circumstances will two students with the same total score get different ability estimates?
  3. If you want to design an adaptive testing system, how can IRT help you?

In-depth study suggestions

  • Try manually calculating a simple likelihood function
  • Think about what the item characteristic curves tested in different subjects might look like.
  • Understand how modern large-scale examinations (such as GRE, TOEFL) apply IRT

docs.title: CTT vs IRT Top Ten Rules Overview
docs.text:
About this chapter

This chapter systematically compares the ten core differences between Classical Measurement Theory (CTT) and Item Response Theory (IRT). Each rule contains a complete derivation process and example analysis.

docs.title: Rule overview table
docs.text: rules CTT perspective IRT perspective core formula Rule 1 standard errorconstant standard error varies from person to person \(SE_{CTT} = \sigma\sqrt{1-r_{tt}}\) vs \(SE_{IRT}(\theta) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{I(\theta)}}\) Rule 2 The longer the better Quality over quantity Spearman-Brown: \(r_{nn} = \frac{nr_{tt}}{1+(n-1)r_{tt}}\) Rule 3 Need parallel testing Personalized Optimal Parallel conditions vs adaptive algorithms Rule 4 sample dependency Sample irrelevant \(p = \int P(\theta)g(\theta)d\theta\) vs \(P(\theta) = \frac{e^{\theta-b}}{1+e^{\theta-b}}\) Rule 5 norm reference item reference Percentile vs ability-item distance Rule 6 by normalization by model Nonlinear transformation vs logit linearity Rule 7 weight imbalance optimal combination Implicit weights vs GPCM Rule 8 initial value dependence Comparable \(r_{DD} = f(r_{12})\) vs MRMLC Rule 9 Phi related questions full information approach \(\phi_{max} < 1\) vs M2PL Rule 10 Features are not important Features can be modeled Black box vs LLTM

docs.title: CTT Basics
docs.text:
CTT core model:

\[ X = T + E \]

Key assumptions:

  1. \(E(E) = 0\)
  2. \(\operatorname{Cov}(T,E) = 0\)
  3. Error is the same for everyone

docs.title: IRT Basics
docs.text:
IRT core model (Rasch):

\[ P(\theta) = \frac{e^{\theta-b}}{1+e^{\theta-b}} \]

Key features:

  1. Probabilistic modeling
  2. individualized accuracy
  3. Parameter separation

docs.title: Rule 1: Measure standard error
docs.text:
Rule comparison

CTT IRT The standard error of measurement error applies to all scores within a specific population The standard error of measurement error varies with score, but can be generalized to multiple groups

docs.title: 1.1 Basic model
docs.text:
Basic assumptions of CTT

\[X = T + E\]
  • \(X\) = observation score
  • \(T\) = True score
  • \(E\) = Measurement error

Three core assumptions: 1. \(E(E) = 0\) 2. \(\rho(T,E) = 0\) 3. \(\rho(E_1,E_2) = 0\)

docs.title: 1.2 Derivation of standard error formula
docs.text:
Step 1: Variance Decomposition

\[\sigma_X^2 = \text{Var}(X) = \text{Var}(T + E) = \sigma_T^2 + \sigma_E^2 + 2\text{Cov}(T,E)\]

Due to \(\text{Cov}(T,E) = 0\):

\[\sigma_X^2 = \sigma_T^2 + \sigma_E^2\]

Step 2: Reliability Definition

\[r_{tt} = \frac{\sigma_T^2}{\sigma_X^2} = \frac{\sigma_T^2}{\sigma_T^2 + \sigma_E^2}\]

Step 3: Solve for error variance

\[\sigma_E^2 = \sigma_X^2 - \sigma_T^2 = \sigma_X^2\left(1 - \frac{\sigma_T^2}{\sigma_X^2}\right) = \sigma_X^2(1 - r_{tt})\]

CTT standard error formula

\[SE_{\text{msmt}} = \sigma_E = \sigma_X\sqrt{1 - r_{tt}}\]

Features: Same for all participants, regardless of ability level

docs.title: 1.3 Numerical Example
docs.text:
Given: \(\sigma = 15\), \(r_{tt} = 0.84\)

\[SE_{\text{msmt}} = 15\sqrt{1 - 0.84} = 15\sqrt{0.16} = 15 \times 0.4 = 6\]

Meaning: No matter the test score is 80 points or 40 points, the measurement error is 6 points.

docs.title: 2.1 Information function
docs.text:
Core concept: information function

\[SE(\theta) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{I(\theta)}}\]

The standard error is inversely proportional to the information function

docs.title: 2.2 Derivation of information function (Rasch model)
docs.text:
Step 1: Log likelihood function

Response to a single item \(u_i \in \{0,1\}\):

\[\ln L_i = u_i \ln P_i(\theta) + (1-u_i) \ln(1-P_i(\theta))\]

Among them:

\[P_i(\theta) = \frac{e^{\theta - b_i}}{1 + e^{\theta - b_i}}\]

Step 2: First Derivative

\[\frac{\partial \ln L_i}{\partial \theta} = u_i - P_i(\theta)\]

Step 3: Second Derivative

\[\frac{\partial^2 \ln L_i}{\partial \theta^2} = -P_i(\theta)[1-P_i(\theta)]\]

Step 4: Fisher Information

item information function

\[I_i(\theta) = -E\left[\frac{\partial^2 \ln L_i}{\partial \theta^2}\right] = P_i(\theta)[1-P_i(\theta)]\]

Maximum information point: When \(P_i(\theta) = 0.5\), \(I_i(\theta) = 0.25\)

docs.title: 2.3 Analysis of the properties of information function
docs.text:
\(P_i(\theta)\) \(I_i(\theta)\) Measurement accuracy 0.5 0.25 highest 0.9 0.09 lower 0.1 0.09 lower 0.99 0.0099 very low

Core Insight: When item difficulty matches ability (\(\theta = b_i\)), the measurement is most accurate.

docs.title: 3.1 Square of average standard error
docs.text: \[\sigma_\theta^2 = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^N [SE(\theta_j)]^2 = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^N \frac{1}{I(\theta_j)}\]

docs.title: 3.2 Trait variation
docs.text: \[\sigma^2 = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^N (\theta_j - \bar{\theta})^2\]

docs.title: 3.3 Composite reliability formula
docs.text:
IRT compound reliability

\[r'_{tt} = 1 - \frac{\sigma_\theta^2}{\sigma^2}\]

Explanation:

  • \(\sigma^2\) = total variation (difference in ability between participants)
  • \(\sigma_\theta^2\) = Variation due to measurement error
  • \(r'_{tt}\) = Proportion of true ability variation that can be explained

docs.title: 4. CTT vs IRT comparison summary
docs.text:
Key differences

CTT limitations:

  • Single standard error, ignoring differences in abilities
  • Reliance on specific samples
  • Inability to differentiate between measurement accuracy at different ability levels

IRT Advantages:

  • individualizedstandard error
  • Sample independent
  • Accurately locate the best measurement interval

docs.title: Rule 2: test length and reliability
docs.text:
Rule comparison

CTT IRT Longer quizzes are more reliable than shorter ones Shorter quizzes may be more reliable than longer ones

docs.title: 1.1 Question setting
docs.text:
core issues

If the test length is increased to \(n\) times, what will the new reliability be?

docs.title: 1.2 Derivation process
docs.text:
Set variables:

  • Original test: length \(k\), reliability \(r_{tt}\)
  • New tests: length \(nk\), reliability \(r_{nn}\) (to be requested)

Step 1: Variance change analysis

Original quiz:

\[\sigma_X^2 = \sigma_T^2 + \sigma_E^2\]

When the length increases by \(n\) times:

  • True fraction variance: \(\sigma_{T_n}^2 = n^2\sigma_T^2\) (perfect correlation, linear superposition)
  • error variance: \(\sigma_{E_n}^2 = n\sigma_E^2\) (independent error, variance superposition)

Step 2: New Quiz Variance
