docs.title: Adaptive Testing with Self-Evaluation
docs.text:
Special Key takeaway

Existing evidence: Examinee self-selected difficulty, background information, historical scores, and free text may all provide information for CAT cold starts; gains are usually concentrated in very short tests, distribution tails, or examinee with accurate prior predictions. Core limitations: The impact of only personalizing the first question is often quickly corrected by subsequent CAT, and the continued use of too narrow or wrong priors may cause bias and false early stopping; the entire process of self-selected items does not steadily improve measurement efficiency. Unresolved issues: The most valuable research gap is not "whether self-information can be used", but how to calibrate the information generated by Examinee into a reliable distribution, and allow it to simultaneously improve real dynamic topic selection and stopping, while maintaining out-of-sample accuracy and uncertainty calibration.

Traditional Computerized Adaptive Testing (CAT) is awkward when selecting the first question: the system has not observed any answers yet, but must give a question first. A common approach is to first give the examinee the same initial ability value, and then choose the question with the most information at that position. This topic studies another route: **Use examinee's judgment of one's own status at the beginning of the test to provide CAT with a small amount of but potentially useful individual information. **

Self-evaluation here is a broad concept, which can be self-reported ability or symptom level, or active selection of item difficulty. It does not presuppose that the examinee will be able to accurately evaluate himself; the real question is under what conditions this signal is useful, and at what cost if used incorrectly.

docs.title: Three types of adjacent but different methods
docs.text:
method examinee what it offers How to use the system How long does control last? Self-adapted testing Choose the difficulty level of the next question each time Administer the item at the selected level Usually throughout the test Self-informed starting point Self-report level, or choose starting difficulty Set initial ability value or first question Only affects the beginning Informative prior questionnaire, historical scores or other auxiliary variables Construct individualized prior distribution Gradually updated with response evidence

These three types of methods share an intuition: examinee or external sources may hold information that has not been observed by standard CAT. But they are not the same design. In particular, a distinction should be made between letting people choose each question and only letting people's judgment help the CAT get started, and then completely handing over to the standard algorithm.

docs.title: The main research line of this topic
docs.text:
What we focus on is the second category and its interface with the third category: in low-risk psychometrics or adaptive learning scenarios, let the examinee provide self-evaluation on the first or previous \(k\) questions, and then return to the original CAT's ability updates, topic selection rules, and stopping rules.

A minimal version can be written as:

\[ s_i \longrightarrow \widehat{\theta}_i^{(0)} \longrightarrow \text{before}k\text{question} \longrightarrow \text{Standard CAT update and topic selection} \longrightarrow SE(\widehat{\theta}_i)\le \varepsilon. \]

Among them, \(s_i\) represents examinee's self-reported result or difficulty selection, \(\widehat{\theta}_i^{(0)}\) represents the resulting initial ability estimate, \(SE\) represents standard error (standard error), and \(\varepsilon\) represents the original accuracy stop threshold. The core hypothesis is: if \(s_i\) contains information related to the true level, CAT can enter the item area suitable for the examinee faster, thereby achieving the same estimation accuracy with fewer items.

Parts that have not been tested in the first paper

"The number of questions will be shortened" is the hypothesis prepared to be tested in this topic, not the conclusion reached in the first paper below. Wise et al. (1991) used a fixed set of 20 questions and could not compare stopping time or test length.

Intensive reading has been completed for all 14 local candidate documents on this topic that have full text, including eight core documents, three supplementary documents and three extended documents. The core literature answers the individualized starting point and prior, the supplementary literature explains the selection process of examinee, and the extended literature completes the overall evidence of hybrid startup, \(a\)-stratified item bank management, and Self-Adapted Testing and CAT.

docs.title: What have you read in the first article?
docs.text:
A Comparison of Self-Adapted and Computer-Adaptive Tests A direct comparison of two 20-question tests:

  • Self-Adapted Testing (SA): The examinee chooses from six difficulty levels before each question;
  • Computerized Adaptive Testing (CA): The computer selects the next question based on previous performance;
  • Both groups received correctness feedback after each question.

The paper found that the SA group had a higher average ability estimate and lower post-test state anxiety, but it took longer and had a larger ability estimate error variance. It proves that "subjective information mastered by examinee may affect the testing process" is worthy of study, and also exposes the problems of validity, accuracy and causal explanation.

docs.title: What have you read in the second article?
docs.text:
Adjusting Computer Adaptive Test Starting Points to Conserve Item Pool Compares common moderate difficulty starting points, average grade starting points, and combined course and grade point average starting points. The supporting information determines only the first question and thereafter the same CAT is restored.

The combined starting point of courses and average grades spreads the first questions over a wider difficulty range, reduces the concentrated exposure of intermediate items, and maintains ability correlation close to the uninformation starting point under most conditions. However, it did not steadily shorten the variable length CAT; in short tests with looser stopping standards, the average number of questions was about one to two more questions. Using the average score alone also creates an exposure spike at the high-difficulty end due to the large number of 4.0 self-reports, indicating that errors or accumulated auxiliary information may simply shift exposure from the middle of the item bank to the tail of the item bank.

docs.title: What have you read in the third article?
docs.text: Empirical Initialization of the Trait Estimator in Adaptive Testing Model the pre-test auxiliary variables as predictor variables of latent ability, and construct the individualized initial point or complete empirical prior accordingly. Instead of first estimating each person's \(\widehat\theta\) and then doing ordinary regression, the paper retains ability as a latent variable and jointly estimates the regression coefficient and prior variance from the complete item-by-item responses. The actual data example uses the logarithmic response time of the previous test to predict the ability of the later vocabulary test, but does not re-compare the question size, accuracy or exposure of the standard CAT and the individualized prior CAT, so it is a prior construction and estimation method paper, not a CAT efficiency experiment.

docs.title: What have you read in Part 4?
docs.text: Computer Adaptive Testing with Empirical Prior Information: A Gibbs Sampler Approach for Ability Estimation Put the empirical prior constructed by the background variables into the initialization and intermediate/final ability estimate of CAT at the same time, and continue to use the maximum amount of information to select topics after each update. Therefore, "not changing the topic selection formula" does not mean "not changing the actual topic selection path." Under correctly specified simulation priors, the full empirical prior mainly improves the estimation of the 5-question short test and extreme abilities; the semi-empirical condition that only changes the starting point is generally weaker. As the number of questions increases, the advantage shrinks, and the original table does not support that the empirical method has a lower RMSE at each ability point. The paper uses a fixed test length, and does not test whether the number of questions can be reduced with the same stopping accuracy, nor does it simulate error self-evaluation, different prior variance or item exposure.

docs.title: What have you read in the fifth article?
docs.text: Combining Text Mining of Long Constructed Responses and Item-Based Measures Let the examinee write down the traumatic experience and symptoms, obtain the individual score through the existing text classifier, then establish the normal prior of \(\theta_n\mid y_n\) and combine it with the IRT questionnaire likelihood. In a sample of 99 people, the classification accuracy of the complete 21 questions increased from 0.94 for IRT-only to 0.97 for Hybrid; the average posterior standard error of the text prior plus 17 questions was approximately equal to the complete 21 questions without text prior. However, the 21 questions are pre-arranged in the same order according to the amount of information at the common diagnosis cut-off point \(-0.15\). Priority does not drive personalized real-time topic selection; the paper also does not report the classification accuracy, coverage rate or error prior risk of the 17 question conditions.

docs.title: What have you read in Chapter 6?
docs.text:
Empirical Priors in Polytomous Computerized Adaptive Tests uses five-level scoring clinical item bank, maximum a posteriori estimation, maximum Fisher information amount selection and common fixed accuracy stopping rule to respectively manipulate the mean bias and variance of individualized prior. Simply moving the center of the unbiased prior to the true capability while maintaining the variance at 1 does not significantly shorten the CAT; the efficiency gain mainly comes from the smaller prior variance. However, a narrow and wrong prior may send the CAT into the low information area of ​​the item bank, resulting in a long test or the exhaustion of the item bank; it may also quickly reach the standard error threshold in the high information area, resulting in a hidden failure of "the question size is very short but the estimate is seriously biased".

The second, more realistic simulation uses the global score given by the clinician to construct an individualized prior. Among 5,000 simulated examinees, the empirical prior shortened the number of questions for 68% of them, with a median reduction of 20% (1 question), but did not bring significant overall bias improvement. Enforcing a minimum number of questions or relaxing the prior can reduce risks, but it will also weaken the benefits of question volume. This article therefore directly supports us to separate the prior mean error, prior variance and the minimum number of questions, and report the bias, coverage rate, error early stopping and item bank exhaustion at the same time, instead of just comparing the average number of questions.

docs.title: What have you read in Chapter 7?
docs.text:
Evaluating the Use of Prior Information to Individualize Start Item Selection is the study currently closest to "changing only the first item" in terms of mechanism. The author first used a simple regression of one completed quality of life domain to predict another domain in 10,084 cancer patient assessments; then only selected the first question of the target CAT at the predicted position, and restored the original process after the first question. When selecting the best single prediction field for each target field, the prediction-observation correlation ranges from 0.31 to 0.72, and 72% to 89% of the predictions are within 1 standard deviation of the observation score; if averaged across all prediction fields, the performance is significantly lower, and the best result in the summary cannot be generalized to any combination of fields.

CAT simulation shows that the benefits of individualized first questions are mainly concentrated in questions 1 to 3 and in patients far away from the overall mean; the average reliability across domains in low partitions increases by 0.11, and most differences disappear after questions 4 to 5. Only the low physical function condition in the fixed-accuracy simulation had a maximum average reduction of 1.4 questions, and the remaining conditions had no more than 0.7 questions. Note also that the simulation uses a controlled starting point of “true score, true score plus or minus 5 or 10 points” and does not feed the person-by-person prediction errors from the empirical regression end-to-end into CAT. Therefore, it is a good demonstration of the local effect of first-question routing, but it does not prove that real auxiliary information can generally shorten the test significantly.

docs.title: What have you read in Chapter 8?
docs.text:
Impact of Informed Starting Value on Longitudinal Computer Adaptive Tests in PROMIS Assessments simulates two longitudinal CATs using the official PROMIS adult and child item banks. The first time uses the standard \(N(0,1)\) prior; the second time sets the first final EAP to the prior mean and the prior standard deviation to 1, 0.75, 0.5, or 0.25. What is changed here is the complete prior instead of just the first question, and the value is the standard deviation: \(SD=0.5\) corresponds to variance 0.25, and \(SD=0.25\) corresponds to variance 0.0625.

When the state changes are small, \(SD=0.5\) often gets the lowest RMSE with the same or less question volume, but the overall improvement is smaller and relies on item bank coverage. When the state changes are large, most adult fields are most accurate at \(SD=1\); the narrowest prior will strongly pull the second estimate back to the old score. Since \(SD=0.25\) is already smaller than the stopping threshold of \(SE<0.3\), the minimum four-question rule makes CAT almost all stop at the fourth question, forming a "shorter but less accurate" test. The most important methodological inspiration of the paper is that the longitudinal prior variance should include both the last scoring error and the true state change variance, and the accuracy of historical scores cannot be directly regarded as the uncertainty of the current state.

docs.title: Three supplementary documents
docs.text:
Literature Why additional reading Current progress Revuelta (2004), Estimating Ability and Item-Selection Strategy in Self-Adapted Testing: A Latent Class Approach Modeling Examinee's topic selection strategy itself as a latent class reminds us that "what difficulty level is chosen" may also be a type of data that needs to be analyzed. Intensive reading completed Wise et al. (2005), An Investigation of the Effects of Self-Adapted Testing on Examinee Effort and Performance in a Low-Stakes Achievement Test Directly examines effort and performance on low-stakes tests, helping to evaluate the premise that examinee will provide self-information carefully and accurately in low-stakes situations. Intensive reading completed Arieli-Attali et al. (2019), Understanding Test Takers' Choices in a Self-Adapted Test: A Hidden Markov Modeling of Process Data Use the hidden Markov model to analyze how the difficulty selection of each question changes with the target conditions and the answering process. It is suitable to establish a process model for the previous question selection data \(k\). Intensive reading completed

The three supplementary documents are not responsible for answering the main question of "whether to shorten the test", but to help understand how examinees are selected, whether low risk equals high investment, and whether the selection strategy should be entered into the measurement model.

docs.title: What have you read in the first supplementary literature?
docs.text:
Estimating Ability and Item-Selection Strategy in Self-Adapted Testing distinguishes two propositions that are often confused. Under the author's sequential model, the potential response of the unrepresented item satisfies missing at random; but if the difficulty selection strategy is related to ability, the strategy parameters and ability parameters are inseparable, and the selection mechanism must still enter the joint likelihood. Only when the two are independent can ability be estimated based solely on the IRT likelihood of actual responses.

An example of 72 high school students completing a fixed 20-question English vocabulary SAT shows that examinee has different selection modes such as maintaining difficulty, adjusting with feedback, and tolerating failure, and the difficulty changes more frequently in the first half than in the second half. Fitting the front and rear halves separately reduces the AIC from about 5468 to 5228, which is against the assumption that the strategy remains unchanged throughout the game. The paper also found that the asymptotic standard error of the fixed item path is about 40% of the complete Bootstrap standard error, suggesting that the entire topic selection and stopping process must be repeated when verifying the self-assessment driven CAT. It did not examine the effects of question size shortening or individualized prior.

docs.title: What have you read in the second part of the supplementary literature?
docs.text:
An Investigation of the Effects of Self-Adapted Testing on Examinee Effort and Performance in a Low-Stakes Achievement Test Compares fixed-item tests, CAT, question-by-question self-selected difficulty S-AT, and game-based S-AT with dynamic points gains and losses in a low-stakes college setting. The four groups were all fixed at 40 questions; test type had no significant impact on average ability, self-reported effort, and response time effort. The overall RTE was approximately .96, indicating that most responses were not judged as quick guesses by the 10-second threshold, but there was no evidence that the option further improved effort above this higher baseline.

This study does not support the hypothesis that "low risk + self-selection will automatically increase motivation", nor does it examine the reduction in question size. When dealing with allocation at the session level, there are only 15 valid sessions, and the non-significant results cannot prove that the four forms are equivalent; the original table also has inconsistencies in the annotations of RTE sample size, SOS degree of freedom, and invigilator effect size. The research is more suitable to support a careful design: testing the routing value, measurement efficiency and motivational experience of self-evaluation signals separately, rather than treating the motivational benefits of the entire topic selection as an established mechanism.

docs.title: What have you read in the third supplementary literature?
docs.text:
Understanding Test Takers' Choices in a Self-Adapted Test A three-state HMM was constructed for 583 adults on 40 choices each at seven levels of difficulty. The selection centers of low, medium, and high potential states approximately correspond to levels 1.33, 3.57, and 6.02, and the self-maintenance probabilities all exceed .90; this shows that small changes in observed levels are often just intra-state fluctuations, and the same person can actually switch states after feedback accumulation.

The higher the pretest, the greater the probability of initially being in the medium or high state; after controlling for the pretest, the performance-goal group is more likely to start in the low state and less likely to leave the low state. When the cumulative accuracy rate is low, the number of transfers increases, and reliability is set to further adjust the transfer direction. However, the most eye-catching 66.1% to 73.8% increase probability in the paper comes from the extreme and sparse accuracy-reliability combination, which belongs to model extrapolation. AIC supports a 62-parameter model with complete goal interaction, while BIC chooses a simpler accuracy-setting reliability model, and cannot claim that complex interactions are unanimously supported by all criteria.

This remains a retrospective process analysis of the complete sequence. It neither lets the HMM drive CAT nor calibrates its states as ability priors. The most direct implication for this project is to ablate a one-time self-assessment, the mean choice over the first \(k\) items, and online HMM filtering separately, while avoiding the use of current or future item outcomes to predict choices that have already occurred.

docs.title: Three obtained extended documents
docs.text:
Literature Position on research route Current progress Frosini et al. (1998), Performing Automatic Exams First use a pre-test similar to self-adapted testing (Self-Adapted Testing, SAT) to determine the starting difficulty, and then enter the rule-based adaptive test; the architecture is very close to "starting with user information first, and then handing back the algorithm." Intensive reading completed Chang and Ying (1999), a-Stratified Multistage Computerized Adaptive Testing The \(a\)-stratified baseline mentioned by the instructor: Use low-discrimination questions in the early stage and retain high-discrimination questions in the later stage. It mainly solves the problem of item bank exposure and security, rather than using individual information to solve cold start. Intensive reading completed Pitkin and Vispoel (2001), Differences Between Self-Adapted and Computerized Adaptive Tests: A Meta-Analysis The comparative results of early Self-Adapted Testing and Computerized Adaptive Testing are summarized to determine the average impact of allowing choices on ability estimate and post-test anxiety. Intensive reading completed

The full texts of the three extended documents have been obtained and intensive reading has been completed. Frosini et al. (1998) supplement the historical evidence of "how to start"; Chang and Ying (1999) are the baseline of item bank management of different mechanisms; Pitkin and Vispoel (2001) provide the overall evidence background. Bass et al. (2026) has been moved into the core literature because of the informed starting value of directly testing longitudinal CAT.

docs.title: What have you read in the first article of extended literature?
docs.text:
Performing Automatic Exams proposes a two-stage automatic exam. In the pre-examination, students select the difficulty level one by one, randomly obtain items at that level, and receive correctness feedback; if they answer at least one question correctly, the formal examination starts from the highest difficulty level, otherwise it decreases one level from the lowest difficulty level selected. There are six fixed questions in the formal stage, and the level will be raised, lowered or maintained based on the score combination of the last two questions; if the remaining questions cannot reach 18/30 even if all the remaining questions are answered correctly, it will be terminated early.

This is not modern IRT-CAT: the system has no underlying ability estimate, individualized prior, item information, or precision measures, and problems are directly assigned higher scores. The paper reporting system completed more than 300 exams and had 100 students take manual and automated exams; 90% of the scores were less than 3 points, but there was no common starting point comparison, complete consistency statistics, question accuracy comparison, or exposure analysis. It proves that there is historical precedent for "users participating in the startup and the algorithm then taking over", but it does not prove that this kind of startup can shorten CAT; the most important revelation for this item is that the pre-test questions must be included in the total burden, and the difficulty selection signal and the actual answer signal must be ablated separately.

docs.title: What have you read in the second extended article?
docs.text:
a-Stratified Multistage Computerized Adaptive Testing illustrates that the information curve of high-discrimination questions is high and narrow: if the early ability estimate deviates from the true ability, the high-\(a\) questions matched by \(\widehat\theta\) may have almost no information at the true \(\theta\). Therefore, the author divides the item bank into four layers from low to high according to \(a\). Let the low \(a\) layer be used in the early stage of the test and the high \(a\) layer in the later stage. In the current layer, the two closest candidates are selected according to \(|b-\widehat\theta|\) and then randomly tested together.

In three sets of fixed length simulations, STR significantly reduced exposure imbalance, the number of low-exposure questions, and test overlap. The overlap of the 40-question and 400-question item bank conditions dropped from 19% of FSH to 11%, which is close to the theoretical lower bound of 10%. However, in the 20-question condition of the real 3PLM parameters, the MSE of STR is .084, which is higher than FSH's .060. It cannot be generally claimed that there is no accuracy cost. When \(L,N\) is fixed, the average exposure rate is always \(L/N\), so the so-called "lower average exposure" in the abstract should not be taken as a conclusion; the method improves the exposure distribution rather than the conserved average value.

There is no self-evaluation or individualized prior in this article, and it cannot guarantee maximum exposure for a single question. Its direct inspiration for this item is to treat \(b\) as individual position matching and \(a\) as uncertainty and item resource allocation issues: an accurate prior may allow high \(a\) questions to be used in advance, while an incorrect or fuzzy prior requires low \(a\) exploration. Subsequently, the fixed \(a\) layer and the posterior-variance-adaptive layer should be ablated and verified using the information at the real ability, Bias, RMSE, coverage rate, question volume and conditional exposure.

docs.title: What have you read in the third extended article?
docs.text:
Differences Between Self-Adapted and Computerized Adaptive Tests synthesizes 19 ability comparisons and 8 posttest-anxiety comparisons from 15 studies. SAT ability estimates were, on average, \(d=.11\) higher than CAT estimates and .12 after reliability correction; posttest anxiety was, on average, \(d=.18\) lower and .19 after correction. Both effects are small. The higher ability estimates could reflect changes in anxiety or perceived control, or item-selection and scoring bias. The meta-analysis did not conduct a mediation analysis and therefore cannot claim that reduced anxiety caused better performance.

This research synthesis also did not incorporate question size, standard error, time taken, or exposure. The Discussion paragraph states that fixed test length SAT is generally less accurate than CAT and cites one study of equivalent accuracy in which SAT took 43% longer, but this was not a pooled effect of the meta-analysis. Of the 19 ability effects, 13 were positive and 6 were negative; although all anxiety effects were positive, there were only 8. The research team is highly centralized, and the paper does not address effect dependence, heterogeneity, publication bias, or small sample \(d\) bias.

The most important gap for this item is that the early evidence mainly compares the two endpoints of "algorithmic full process control" and "examinee full process control". There is no systematic inspection that only allows users to influence the first question or the first \(k\) question, and then the intermediate design taken over by individualized prior and CAT. Follow-up experiments should orthogonally separate the duration of control, prioritization into estimation, topic selection rules and feedback, and simultaneously measure anxiety, sense of control, question volume, accuracy and item bank exposure.

docs.title: Questions to be answered for subsequent reading
docs.text:
1. Should self-reported information be mapped to a point estimate or a prior distribution with uncertainty?
  2. Which interface is more stable, let the examinee choose the first question, the previous question \(k\), or just report its own level?
  3. When a self-assessment error occurs, how many questions does a standard CAT require to correct the starting point of the error?
  4. Under the same stopping rule, how do the average question volume, tail question volume, bias, root mean squared error (root mean square error, RMSE) and coverage rate change?
  5. Do efficiency gains only occur in examinees at extreme levels of ability or symptoms?
  6. Will changes in the sense of autonomy, anxiety, and motivation change the answering process of the tested construct itself?

The local PDF reading queue for this topic has been completed. Existing evidence focuses the research space into a testable intermediate design: construct an individualized prior with uncertainty using calibrated self-assessment, allowing the user to only affect the first question or the first \(k\) question, and then the standard or uncertainty-driven CAT takes over; under the same stopping accuracy, use complete ablation to simultaneously test question volume, bias, RMSE, coverage rate, psychological experience and conditional exposure.

docs.title: Arieli-Attali et al. (2019): Using hidden Markov model to understand question-by-question difficulty selection
docs.text:
Key takeaway

What was done: Arieli-Attali et al. used the item-by-item difficulty selection, correctness and error, reliability and feedback data of 583 examinees to establish a three-state hidden Markov model, and summarized the selection process into three difficulty preference states of low, medium and high that can be converted with the item. What was gained: Target instructions, cumulative accuracy and cumulative placement reliability can predict the initial state and state transition, indicating that difficulty selection is neither a fixed personality category nor a simple "upgrade for correct answers and downgrade for incorrect answers". Conclusion on this topic: Self-selected difficulty contains dynamic process information, but these states cannot be directly regarded as abilities or prior; this article only provides post-mortem explanations and does not allow HMM to drive CAT topic selection.

docs.title: Citation details
docs.text:
Arieli-Attali, M., Ou, L., & Simmering, V. R. (2019). Understanding test takers' choices in a self-adapted test: A hidden Markov modeling of process data. Frontiers in Psychology, 10, Article 83. DOI

  • Research type: Secondary process analysis of existing randomized experimental data
  • Sample: 583 U.S. or Canadian native English-speaking adults
  • Test: 24-question fixed pre-test plus 40-question adaptive general knowledge test
  • Process data: seven levels of difficulty, correct or incorrect, 0–100 placement reliability and feedback for each question
  • Manipulated variables: performance goal and learning goal
  • Core method: three-state hidden Markov model (Hidden Markov Model, HMM)
  • Main conclusion: The selection sequence can be summarized into three relatively stable potential difficulty preference states of low, medium and high; target conditions, cumulative accuracy and cumulative placement reliability jointly predict the initial state and state transition

The easiest place to read this article wrong

The paper does not let HMM drive CAT topic selection, nor does it turn the potential state into an individualized prior. It is a post hoc explanatory model of the complete 40-item choice sequence. The eye-catching transition probabilities such as 66.1% or 73.8% in the article are model predictions calculated on extreme and sparse correct rate-position reliability combinations, and are not common observation proportions in the sample.

docs.title: 1. How is this article an improvement over Revuelta (2004)?
docs.text:
Revuelta (2004) treats each person as using one potential selection strategy for the entire field, but his actual data have shown that exploration in the first half, stability in the second half, and static category assumptions are not good enough.

This study allows the same person to change potential states in question order:

\[ S_{i1} \rightarrow S_{i2} \rightarrow \cdots \rightarrow S_{i40}. \]

Each state produces a period of different levels of difficulty choices, and the previous state, target conditions, cumulative accuracy and cumulative reliability determine the probability of the next state.

Therefore, the study population starts from:

\[ \text{“Which strategy does this person fall into?”} \]

Steering:

\[ \text{"This person is in the}t\text{What status is the question in and when will it be converted? "} \]

This is suitable for analyzing the dynamic self-assessment signal in the previous question \(k\).

docs.title: 2. Why the choice of difficulty may have multiple psychological sources
docs.text:
Also choose high difficulty, which may come from:

-Higher real ability; - A high estimate of one's abilities; - Like challenges; - Active exploration under learning goal; - Overconfidence; - Strategic responses to feedback.

The same choice of low difficulty may also come from:

  • Low real ability;
  • Lack of self-confidence;
  • Hope to maximize the number of correct answers;
  • Reduce stress;
  • Complete the task with minimum effort.

So choice level is not a pure measure of ability. The author introduces Feeling of Knowledge (FOK) and goal orientation into the model, trying to distinguish how external correct feedback and internal confidence judgment jointly promote choice changes.

docs.title: 3. What experiment does the data come from?
3.1 Sample
docs.text:
Data from Arieli-Attali (2016):

  • \(N=583\)；
  • Age 18–74 years, mean 33.09 years;
  • 45% female;
  • Recruited via Amazon Mechanical Turk;
  • Native English speakers and residents of the United States or Canada only.

The original experiment lasted for two days, and this article only uses the data from day 1.

docs.title: 3.2 Fixed pre-test
docs.text:
Participants first completed 24 non-adaptive open-ended general knowledge questions. The range of pre-test accuracy is:

\[ .22\text{to}1.00, \qquad M=.75, \qquad SD=.16. \]

docs.title: 3.3 Random target conditions
docs.text:
Then randomly divided into:

  • Performance goal: 286 people were asked to maximize their test scores and were given incentives;
  • learning goal: 297 people were asked to use the test on that day as a learning tool for the test on the next day.

Therefore, between-group differences in target conditions are closer to causal explanations than within-group correlations between accuracy and reliability.

docs.title: 3.4 40 questions self-adapted testing
docs.text:
The process for each question is:

  1. Choose difficulty from seven levels;
  2. Answer an open-ended general knowledge question;
  3. Report reliability as 0, 10, 20, ..., 100;
  4. Get correctness feedback and correct answers after submission;
  5. Select the difficulty level of the next question.

Correct is recorded as 1 and incorrect as 0; set reliability and scale it to \([0,1]\); divide the difficulty level by 7 to convert it to a value of approximately \([.14,1]\).

The author mentioned that the original experiment also studied different feedback conditions, but this HMM did not include this factor into the model. If the feedback manipulation affects choice shifting, this omission may leave some of the variance in the residuals or other covariates.

docs.title: 4. How difficult are the seven difficulty levels?
docs.text:
The average IRT difficulty and average correct answer probability of the seven-layer items are:

level average item difficulty average probability of correct answer 1 -3.3 92% 2 -1.8 80% 3 -0.9 68% 4 -0.2 55% 5 0.5 41% 6 1.0 30% 7 1.8 16%

The author treats the seven-level selection as a continuous variable because the number of categories reaches seven and it can approximate a continuous difficulty axis.

The level numbers are equidistant, but the actual \(b\) is not

The model uses a normal emission distribution for \(1/7,2/7,\ldots,7/7\), which is equivalent to treating adjacent grade spacing as the same. However, the actual average intervals of \(b\) are approximately 1.5, 0.9, 0.7, 0.7, 0.5 and 0.8, which are not equidistant. If the research goal is to precisely connect selection to item parameters, it would be more natural to use the actual \(b\) or ordered category emission model.

docs.title: 5.1 Observation layer: How does the potential state generate difficulty selection?
docs.text:
Remember that the potential state of individual \(i\) in question \(j\) is:

\[ S_{ij}\in\{1,\ldots,M\}, \]

The observed difficulty choice is \(Y_{ij}\). The author assumes:

\[ Y_{ij}\mid S_{ij}=m \sim N(\mu_m,\sigma_m^2). \]

After the potential state is given, the selection conditions of each question are independent. The larger the state mean value is, the more difficult the question is that the examinee tends to choose at that point in time.

docs.title: 5.2 State layer: how the state changes over time
docs.text:
The potential state satisfies a first-order Markov process:

\[ P(S_{ij}\mid S_{i,1:j-1}) = P(S_{ij}\mid S_{i,j-1},\mathbf h_{ij}). \]

Here \(\mathbf h_{ij}\) is a covariate that changes with the question. Although the state only directly depends on the previous state, the cumulative accuracy and cumulative reliability compress the earlier history into covariates, so this is not "completely forgetting the earlier items", but retaining the history through summaries.

docs.title: 6. Initial state model
docs.text:
Initial state probabilities use multinomial logistic regression:

\[ P(S_{i1}=m\mid\mathbf I_i) = \frac{ \exp(a_m+\mathbf b_m^\top\mathbf I_i) }{ \sum_{k=1}^{M} \exp(a_k+\mathbf b_k^\top\mathbf I_i) }. \]

The covariates are:

\[ \mathbf I_i = (d_i,p_i,d_ip_i), \]

Among them:

  • \(d_i\): target conditions, performance=1, learning=0;
  • \(p_i\): 24 questions pre-test accuracy rate;
  • \(d_ip_i\): The two interact.

This part asks how target instructions and existing ability performance change the starting probabilities of low, medium, and high states before seeing the first self-choice question.

docs.title: 7. State transition model
docs.text:
The probability of going from the previous state \(l\) to the current state \(m\) is:

\[ P(S_{ij}=m\mid S_{i,j-1}=l,\mathbf h_{ij}) = \frac{ \exp(c_{lm}+\mathbf d_{lm}^\top\mathbf h_{ij}) }{ \sum_{k=1}^{M} \exp(c_{lk}+\mathbf d_{lk}^\top\mathbf h_{ij}) }. \]

The covariates for the full model are:

\[ \mathbf h_{ij} = (d,r,f,dr,df,rf,drf), \]

Among them:

  • \(r\): cumulative average accuracy;
  • \(f\): cumulative average reliability;
  • The rest are second- and third-order interactions.

The model is estimated by depmixS4 using the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm; the Viterbi algorithm is used to give the most likely state path.

docs.title: 8. Why does the number of model parameters increase so quickly?
docs.text:
For \(M\) states, the complete number of model parameters is:

\[ 2M + 4(M-1) + 8M(M-1). \]

The three parts are:

  1. Each state has a mean and a variance, totaling \(2M\);
  2. \(M-1\) logistic equations in the initial state, each containing an intercept and three covariates, totaling \(4(M-1)\);
  3. Transition equations from each source state to \(M-1\) non-reference target states, each containing an intercept and seven covariates, totaling \(8M(M-1)\).

When \(M=3\):

\[ 6+8+48=62 \]

parameters, consistent with the full model B3 in Table 1. The large number of higher-order interactions makes interpretation dependent on plotting predicted probabilities rather than reading regression coefficients directly.

docs.title: 9. What does the original selection sequence tell us first?
9.1 People who are fixed at extreme levels
docs.text:
Always choose level 1 for the entire 40-question session:

  • Performance goal: 33 people, accounting for 11.54%;
  • learning goal: 10 people, accounting for 3.37%.

Always choose level 7 throughout the game:

  • performance goal: 3 people, accounting for 1.05%;
  • learning goal: 5 people, accounting for 1.68%.

The learning group was significantly less likely to take the “easiest of the whole” path.

docs.title: 9.2 learning group switches more often
docs.text:
Average number of observed grade increases:

\[ 7.43\text{（learning）} \quad\text{vs.}\quad 6.07\text{（performance）}. \]

Average number of downward adjustments:

\[ 6.51\text{（learning）} \quad\text{vs.}\quad 5.40\text{（performance）}. \]

docs.title: 9.3 Select distribution
docs.text: Among all \(583\times40=23{,}320\) choices, level 1 accounts for 22.85%, level 4 accounts for 19.67%, and level 3 accounts for 16.13%; the difficulty selection is not a unimodal normal distribution, but more like a mixture of multiple preference distributions.

docs.title: 9.4 Correlation of three variables
docs.text:
\[ \operatorname{Cor}(\text{Difficulty selection},\text{Correct})=-.30, \] \[ \operatorname{Cor}(\text{Difficulty selection},\text{Confidence})=-.28, \] \[ \operatorname{Cor}(\text{Correct},\text{Confidence})=.60, \]

Both report \(p<.001\). When the choice is more difficult, the correct answer rate and reliability are on average lower; correctness and confidence are generally more consistent.

docs.title: 9.5 Why is sequence model needed?
docs.text:
After removing participant and item effects, the average first-order autocorrelation of difficulty selection residuals is approximately:

\[ \rho_1\approx.44. \]

There is a clear time dependence between the choices, and the 23,320 choices cannot be treated as independent observations.

docs.title: 10. Why choose three states in the end?
docs.text:
The two-state and three-state models without covariates are:

model Number of states AIC BIC A 2 -16658.95 -16602.55 B 3 -27223.54 -27110.74

Both AIC and BIC clearly support the three-state model. The three emission distributions are:

\[ \mu_L=.19,\quad \sigma_L=.07, \] \[ \mu_M=.51,\quad \sigma_M=.12, \] \[ \mu_H=.86,\quad \sigma_H=.13. \]

After multiplying back to 7, the state center approximately corresponds to the observation level:

\[ 1.33,quad3.57,quad6.02. \]

So low, medium, and high are concise labels for difficulty selection preferences.

Latent state is not a validated psychological construct

The three states are low, medium, and high difficulty preferences identified from the choice distribution. The authors further interpret them as self-assessed abilities and/or motivational states, but there are no external scales or experimental manipulations to verify these two meanings respectively. To call it a "low ability state" or a "low motivation state" would be more than the data supports.

docs.title: 11. How stable are the three states?
docs.text:
The transfer matrix for model B without covariates is approximately:

\[ \mathbf P= \begin{pmatrix} .93 & .05 & .02\\ .04 & .92 & .04\\ .04 & .06 & .90 \end{pmatrix}. \]

Rows represent the current state and columns represent the next state. All three states have self-maintenance probabilities of at least .90.

This explains an apparent contradiction: the observed rank may frequently change from 3 to 4 or from 6 to 5, but these changes may simply be random fluctuations in the same underlying preference state and do not imply a true shift in motivation or self-judgment.

The same observation level can also belong to different potential states. For example, if level 4 is sandwiched in a series of high-difficulty choices, it may be judged by the HMM as an accidental low choice of high status; if it appears after a lower sequence, it may belong to the medium status.

docs.title: 12. The initial state is affected by pretest and target conditions
docs.text:
The B1 model that adds pretest, target conditions, and interactions fits better than the B model without covariates:

\[ \Delta\chi^2=71.26, \qquad \Delta df=6, \qquad p<.05. \]

The main modes are:

  • The higher the pre-test, the greater the probability of initially being in a medium or high state;
  • After controlling for the pretest, the performance group has a higher probability of initially being in a low state;
  • Below about 50% on the pretest, both groups have more than half the predicted probability of entering the low state.

For example, when the pretest is .50, the low state probability given in Figure 6 is approximately:

\[ .619\text{（performance）} \quad\text{vs.}\quad .507\text{（learning）}. \]

This shows that the difficulty selection of the first question contains both ability clues and goal orientation clues. Directly equating choice levels with ability would misinterpret preference differences caused by experimental instructions as ability differences.

docs.title: 13. How target conditions affect state transitions
docs.text:
B2a, which only adds the target condition to the transition model, has a better likelihood ratio test than B1:

\[ \Delta\chi^2=35.89, \qquad \Delta df=6, \qquad p<.05. \]

Starting from a low state:

Conditions stay in low state Go to mid state Go to high state performance .943 .041 .016 learning .906 .071 .023

The total probability of upgrading from a low state is about .094 for the learning group and about .057 for the performance group. The transitions from the medium and high states of the two groups are very similar.

Thus, the difference in goal conditions was not primarily about making people in all positions upregulate generally, but rather making people in the low-difficulty preference state more likely to leave the low state.

docs.title: 14. How accuracy and reliability jointly predict transfers
docs.text:
B2b uses cumulative accuracy \(r\), cumulative reliability \(f\) and interactive prediction transfer, compared to B1:

\[ \Delta\chi^2=219.83, \qquad \Delta df=18, \qquad p<.05. \]

The main modes are:

  1. When the cumulative accuracy rate is high, most people remain in the original state regardless of reliability;
  2. When the cumulative accuracy rate is low, both up and down transfers increase;
  3. When the accuracy rate is low and the confidence is low, the prediction probability of downgrading from the medium state is 22.3%;
  4. When the accuracy rate is low and the confidence is high, the prediction probability of downgrading from the high state is 27.7%;
  5. Also at the extreme point of low accuracy and high confidence, the total prediction probability of upward adjustment from the low state reaches 66.1%.

Point 5 may seem counter-intuitive: People who have answered a lot of questions wrong but are still very confident may actually jump up from a low state. The author borrows the attention/surprise mechanism explanation of hypercorrection and believes that high-confidence error feedback may make people change strategies or increase effort.

66.1% is an extreme prediction, not a common observation frequency

Figure 8 shows the continuous model using the four extreme combinations of "all wrong answers/all correct answers" and "lowest/highest reliability". Figure 9 shows that as the number of questions increases, the accuracy and reliability are increasingly clustered on the diagonal, and the samples in the overconfidence and underconfidence quadrants are very sparse. So 66.1% is sensitive to parameter form and extrapolation and should not be written as "about two-thirds of overconfident people adjust the difficulty".

docs.title: 15. Complete interaction model and model selection differences
docs.text:
B3 adds the target conditions and all second-order and third-order interactions with accuracy and reliability to the transition model. Compared to B2b:

\[ \Delta\chi^2=68.67, \qquad \Delta df=24, \qquad p<.05. \]

When the accuracy is extremely low, the confidence is high, and starting from a low state, the upward adjustment probability is approximately:

\[ 73.8\%\text{（performance）} \quad\text{vs.}\quad 65.2\%\text{（learning）}. \]

The full model also predicts more upregulation in the performance group at the extreme points of high accuracy, low confidence.

However, different criteria give different conclusions:

model Shift predictors Number of parameters AIC BIC B1 No new transfer predictors 20 -27282.80 -27121.66 B2a goal condition 26 -27306.69 -27097.20 B2b Accuracy, placement reliability and interaction 38 -27466.63 -27160.46 B3 goal, accuracy, reliability and all interactions 62 -27487.31 -26987.77

AIC supports the most complex B3; BIC explicitly supports B2b and considers B2a to be worse than B1 and B3 to be worse than B2b. The authors acknowledge these two BIC reversals in footnotes.

How to quote model selection result

It can be said that goal interaction improves fit under LRT versus AIC, but it cannot be said that all model selection evidence supports full B3. If the research purpose is robust prediction or online use, the simplicity advantage of B2b deserves priority verification; high-order goal interactions require independent samples or cross-validation.

docs.title: 16. A chronological ambiguity that requires special checking
docs.text:
The research goal and discussion of the paper say that the accuracy and reliability of the "previous item" are used to predict the next state transition. But the method section also says: The cumulative accuracy and reliability of question \(j\) are calculated based on "from the beginning to question \(j\)", and \(\mathbf h_{ij}\) is used to predict the transfer from \(S_{i,j-1}\) to \(S_{ij}\).

If the implementation actually includes item \(j\) itself, temporal leakage occurs: the difficulty of item \(j\) is selected before that item's correctness and confidence are observed, so they cannot be used to predict the state of item \(j\) in real time.

The original text did not resolve this ambiguity with a code or a more precise index. Subsequent reproductions should explicitly use:

\[ r_{i,j-1} = \frac{1}{j-1} \sum_{t=1}^{j-1}U_{it}, \] \[ f_{i,j-1} = \frac{1}{j-1} \sum_{t=1}^{j-1}C_{it}, \]

to predict \(S_{ij}\) instead of containing the current question result.

docs.title: 17. Why can’t HMM status directly become prior?
docs.text:
HMM estimate for this article:

\[ P(S_{ij}\mid Y_{i,1:40},\text{covariates}), \]

What CAT prior requires is:

\[ p(\theta_i\mid\text{Pre-test or currently available information}). \]

There is still a proven bridge between the two:

\[ S_{ij} \longrightarrow p(\theta_i\mid S_{ij}). \]

Although low, medium, and high states are related to pretest scores, states are also affected by goal instructions, confidence bias, and feedback responses. If set directly:

\[ \mu_L<\mu_M<\mu_H \]

And by treating them as prior means of ability, it is possible to miscalculate motivation or risk preference as ability.

A safe approach is to jointly estimate using independent calibration samples:

\[ \theta_i\mid S_{it}=m \sim N(\mu_m,\tau_m^2), \]

And check the bias, coverage rate and error state transfer risk in the verification sample.

docs.title: 18. Direct inspiration for the self-assessment design of the previous \(k\) question
18.1 Separate comparison of static self-evaluation and dynamic status
docs.text:
Recommended ablation:

  1. Only use the first difficulty selection;
  2. Use the average value of \(k\) question selection before use;
  3. Use HMM with selection plus correct error;
  4. Use HMM of selection, error and reliability;
  5. Add or not add target/situation variables.

Only in this way can we judge whether the complex dynamic model really exceeds the simple starting point.

docs.title: 18.2 Filtering is required for online use, and no peeking into the future is allowed.
docs.text:
The Viterbi path shown in the paper is a post hoc decoding of the complete sequence. Online CAT at step \(t\) can only be used:

\[ p(S_{it}\mid Y_{i,1:t}, U_{i,1:t-1}, C_{i,1:t-1}). \]

The choices after question \(t+1\) cannot be used to re-judge the current status. A clear distinction should be made in the simulation:

  • filtering: only use current and past information, deployable;
  • Smoothing/Viterbi: Utilize longer sequences, suitable for post hoc interpretation.

docs.title: 18.3 Setting reliability may increase information and interaction burden.
docs.text:
Asking about reliability for each question can help identify "correct answers but not confident" and "wrong answers but confident", but it will increase the test length and response burden. Comparable:

  • Ask only in the first question;
  • Ask the previous question \(k\);
  • Ask every few questions;
  • No questions at all, just answers and choices.

docs.title: 18.4 Choosing a path creates a feedback loop
docs.text:
\[ \text{Choose difficulty} \rightarrow \text{item difficulty} \rightarrow \text{correct and confident} \rightarrow \text{next time choice}. \]

Therefore, the relationship between accuracy, placement reliability and transfer is an endogenous correlation within the system, and is not a simple effect of "increasing placement reliability will cause an increase in causality". To identify causal mechanisms requires random manipulation of feedback, confidence cues, or target conditions.

docs.title: 18.5 Dynamic state should trigger safety mechanism instead of direct force contraction
docs.text:
A testable design is:

  • When the state posterior is concentrated and consistent with the answer, narrower prior or higher \(a\) questions are allowed to be opened earlier;
  • When the status is uncertain or conflicts with the answer, the prior variance is expanded;
  • The extreme overconfidence state is only used for exploratory routing and does not trigger early stopping;
  • Set a minimum number of questions to prevent error states from causing short and biased tests.

This use of the HMM as a "self-rated reliability controller" is more reliable than directly translating H/M/L into capability scores.

docs.title: 19. This paper proves nothing
docs.text:
This article has not tested:

  • Whether HMM shortens CAT;
  • Whether HMM status improves the accuracy of ability estimate;
  • Can the potential state construct a calibration prior;
  • Whether using status topic selection improves exposure;
  • Can the three-state structure be replicated across item bank, age, or mental health constructs;
  • Whether the full B3 outperforms the simpler model on new samples;
  • Whether the state probability is used as the basis for stopping has the correct coverage rate.

It demonstrates that a three-state HMM can provide interpretable dynamic summaries of this set of 40 question choice sequences and reveal patterns of association between goals, performance, and confidence.

docs.title: 20. Chinese paraphrases that can be quoted safely
About dynamic strategy
docs.text: Arieli-Attali et al. (2019) used a three-state HMM to summarize the seven-level question-by-question difficulty selection into low, medium, and high difficulty preference states, and allowed the same examinee to transition between states with the order of questions.

docs.title: About state stability
docs.text: The self-maintenance probabilities for the three states in the covariate-free model are all above .90, indicating that many changes in observed levels are random fluctuations within the same underlying preference state rather than true changes in psychological state.

docs.title: About target conditions
docs.text: After controlling for pretest performance, the performance-goal group is more likely to start from a low-difficulty state and is less likely to transition upward from a low state; the difference between groups starting from a medium and high state is small.

docs.title: About correctness and confidence
docs.text: When the cumulative accuracy rate is low, state transitions increase, and there is an interaction between accuracy rate and reliability; however, the large transition probability in extreme overconfidence conditions comes from model predictions in sparse areas and should be interpreted with caution.

docs.title: About evidence boundaries
docs.text: This study is a post hoc HMM analysis of the selection process and does not let the latent state drive the online CAT, nor does it prove that the state can be directly converted into individualized capabilities prior.

docs.title: 21. How to divide the work of key references
docs.text: Literature role in this article Koriat（1993, 2000） Feeling of Knowledge and Confidence Judgments Dweck and Leggett（1988）；Dweck（2006） performance and learning goal theory Arieli-Attali（2016） Original experiment, item bank and main group results Rocklin and O'Donnell（1987） Proposal of S-AT Revuelta（2004） Static latent class selection model Vermunt et al.（1999） Latent Markov model with covariates Visser and Speekenbrink（2010） depmixS4 Software and Estimation Viterbi（1967） most likely state path algorithm Butterfield and Metcalfe（2001, 2006） High confidence errors and hypercorrection explanations

docs.title: 22. Summary
docs.text:
Revuelta (2004) tells us that there is heterogeneity in selection strategies; Arieli-Attali et al. (2019) further explains that strategies also change over time:

\[ \boxed{ \text{topic by topic selection} = \text{latent preference status} + \text{Fluctuation within the state} + \text{Conversions influenced by feedback and goals} } \]

This is important for our study because first question choice is not necessarily a stable, pure signal of ability. It is affected by pretest ability, goal instruction, cumulative success, and confidence calibration.

HMM can help determine whether the self-evaluation signal is stable, consistent with the answers, and when the prior should be relaxed; however, the paper did not complete the calibration from status to ability prior, nor did it verify the benefits of online topic selection. The next methodological question is not to simply replicate the HMM, but to compare: how much predictive value is added by the dynamic state relative to a self-evaluation, and whether these increments are sufficient to compensate for the additional interaction burden and model risk.

docs.title: Bass et al. (2026): Can longitudinal PROMIS CAT use the previous score as prior
docs.text:
Key takeaway

What was done: In a two-time-point PROMIS CAT simulation, Bass et al. set the final score of the first CAT to the prior mean of the second measurement and systematically varied the prior standard deviation. What you get: When health status changes are small, a moderately shrinking prior may shorten the test slightly and reduce RMSE; when changes are large, a too narrow prior will lock the estimate around the old score, making the test appear to stop faster but missing the real change. Conclusions for this topic: The individualized prior variance is as important as the mean, short tests cannot be considered successful alone, error, variation recovery and error early stopping must be checked simultaneously.

docs.title: Citation details
docs.text:
Bass, M., Morris, S., & Lam, T. (2026). Brief reports: Impact of informed starting value on longitudinal computer adaptive tests in PROMIS assessments. Advances in Patient-Reported Outcomes, 2, 100322. DOI

  • Study type: Two-time point test-retest CAT simulation
  • Application tools: Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) adult and pediatric item bank
  • Supporting information: Final \(\widehat\theta_1\) for first CAT
  • The second CAT: use \(\widehat\theta_1\) as the prior mean and change the prior standard deviation
  • Estimation method: expected a posteriori estimation (Expected A Posteriori, EAP)
  • stopping rule: at least 4 questions, \(SE<0.3\), at most 8 questions
  • Main conclusion: Moderately weighting old scores may slightly shorten the test and reduce RMSE when health status changes are small; too narrow a prior will lock the second estimate near the old score, resulting in a shorter but less accurate test

The easiest place to read this article wrong

The title uses informed starting value, but what the authors change is the full prior distribution of the second CAT. It not only determines the starting position, but also continues into the EAP ability estimate, question-by-question selection, final score, and stopping judgement. Therefore it is not a “just change the first question” study like Petersen et al.’s (2026) study.

docs.title: 1. Research question: Why doesn’t the retest start directly from the last score?
docs.text:
Longitudinal CAT already has scores from the last measurement of the same patient. The most natural idea is:

\[ \mu_{2,p} = \widehat\theta_{1,p}. \]

If patient status does not change much, this is more personalized than starting from a population mean of 0 each time.

The problem is that the last score is not equal to the true state this time:

\[ \theta_{2,p} = \theta_{1,p} + \delta_p, \]

where \(\delta_p\) is the true change between the two evaluations. In addition, \(\widehat\theta_{1,p}\) itself has measurement errors.

If the system only uses the final standard error of the last measurement as the prior uncertainty, it implicitly assumes:

\[ \delta_p=0. \]

In situations where there is a real need to monitor response, progression, or recovery, this assumption may not hold true. Overconfidence in old scores shrinks the second estimate toward the old state, reducing the ability to detect changes.

docs.title: 2. The vertical prior variance should include two types of uncertainty
docs.text:
The author uses a simple approximation to express the uncertainty of the second state relative to the first estimate:

\[ SD(\theta_2\mid\widehat\theta_1) = \sqrt{ SE(\widehat\theta_1)^2 + SD(\delta)^2 }. \]

Included here:

  1. The scoring error of the last CAT is \(SE(\widehat\theta_1)\);
  2. Individual differences in true change between two measurements \(SD(\delta)\).

This formula is valuable to us because it illustrates that the variance of individualized priors cannot be determined solely by "how accurate the self-assessment itself appears to be." If there is a time gap, situation change or construct drift between the auxiliary information and the current target state, the uncertainty of the state change must also be added.

docs.title: An intuitive numerical example
docs.text:
The final standard error of PROMIS for the first measurement is about \(0.25\), and if there is a small change between the two times the standard deviation is about \(0.30\):

\[ \sqrt{0.25^2+0.30^2} \approx 0.39. \]

The closest simulated candidate value is prior \(SD=0.5\).

If the standard deviation of the change is \(0.80\):

\[ \sqrt{0.25^2+0.80^2} \approx 0.84. \]

At this time \(SD=0.75\) or \(1.0\) is more reasonable. The paper results also generally show this pattern: \(0.5\) is often the best when there are small changes, and \(0.75\) or \(1.0\) is safer when there are big changes.

The author also proposed that if we have large-sample longitudinal data of the appropriate population, we can directly estimate the change variance; if not, we can set it based on existing research, retest intervals and expert judgment, and then adjust parameters through simulation.

docs.title: 3. Prior standard deviation and prior variance must be distinguished
docs.text:
Bass et al manipulated:

\[ SD_{\mathrm{prior}} \in \{1.00,0.75,0.50,0.25\}. \]

The corresponding variance is:

\[ \operatorname{Var}_{\mathrm{prior}} \in \{1.00,0.5625,0.25,0.0625\}. \]

This is consistent with the prior variance manipulated by Frans et al. (2023):

\[ \{1.00,0.50,0.25\} \]

Not the same set of strengths.

Bass：prior SD Bass：prior variance Approximately corresponding meaning 1.00 1.0000 Little trust in old scores 0.75 0.5625 light trust 0.50 0.2500 medium trust 0.25 0.0625 Strong trust

Directly related to our \(\tau^2\) experiment

If we say "prior variance from 0.1 to 1", Bass's \(SD=0.25\) is not variance 0.25, but variance 0.0625; \(SD=0.5\) only corresponds to variance 0.25. Comparisons across papers must be unified to variance or precision, and surface numbers cannot be directly compared.

docs.title: 4. Which PROMIS item banks are used for simulation
Seven adult areas
docs.text:
1. Physical Function；
  2. Fatigue；
  3. Pain Interference；
  4. Sleep Disturbance；
  5. Depression；
  6. Anxiety；
  7. Ability to Participate in Social Roles and Activities。

docs.title: Six children’s areas
docs.text:
1. Mobility；
  2. Fatigue；
  3. Pain Interference；
  4. Depressive Symptoms；
  5. Anxiety；
  6. Peer Relationships。

A practical advantage of the paper is to use the official PROMIS item bank and actual running software, instead of just generating a fictitious item bank according to rough parameters. The item bank for adults and children differs in the number of questions, coverage, and ceiling/floor effects. It can be tested whether the prior income is limited by the characteristics of the item bank.

docs.title: 5. How to generate data at two time points
5.1 The true state of Time 1
docs.text:
The first measured true capability is located at nine grid points:

\[ \theta_{1,p} \in \{-2,-1.5,-1,-0.5,0,0.5,1,1.5,2\}. \]

Each grid point is simulated 100 times, so each PROMIS field has:

\[ 900 \]

Group assessment.

docs.title: 5.2 Real changes in Time 2
docs.text: The authors simulate two scales of change:

docs.title: Small changes
docs.text: \[ \delta_p\sim N(0,0.3), \]

docs.title: Big changes
docs.text:
\[ \delta_p\sim N(0,0.8). \]

The text discusses \(0.3\) and \(0.8\) as the standard deviation/effect size scale of variation, although the second parameter of \(N(0,\cdot)\) is not clearly written as variance or standard deviation in the symbol. This page will be recorded as \(SD(\delta)=0.3\) or \(0.8\) according to the author's textual explanation.

So:

\[ \theta_{2,p} = \theta_{1,p} + \delta_p. \]

The paper allows for both improvement and deterioration since the change distribution is centered around 0.

docs.title: 6. Prior, estimation and stopping rule of two CATs
Time 2
docs.text:
The prior mean is set to the final EAP of the first CAT:

\[ \mu_{2,p} = \widehat\theta_{1,p}. \]

Then use:

\[ \theta_{2,p} \sim N( \widehat\theta_{1,p}, \sigma_{\mathrm{prior}}^2 ), \]

Among them:

\[ \sigma_{\mathrm{prior}} \in \{1.00,0.75,0.50,0.25\}. \]

Each domain implements CAT separately, item responses are generated by the corresponding IRT model in that domain, and ability estimate uses EAP. prior will continue to participate in the posterior of the second CAT:

\[ p(\theta_{2,p}\mid\mathbf u_{2,p}) \propto p(\mathbf u_{2,p}\mid\theta_{2,p}) \phi( \theta_{2,p}; \widehat\theta_{1,p}, \sigma_{\mathrm{prior}}^2 ). \]

Therefore prior affects:

\[ \text{initial position} \rightarrow \text{Question 1} \rightarrow \text{Follow-up EAP} \rightarrow \text{Follow-up topic selection} \rightarrow \text{Final estimate and stop}. \]

The common stopping rules are:

\[ n\geq4, \qquad SE(\widehat\theta)<0.3, \qquad n\leq8. \]

The evaluation indicators are:

  • Average number of questions;
  • Final estimated root mean squared error (root mean squared error, RMSE):
\[ \operatorname{RMSE} = \sqrt{ \frac{1}{N} \sum_{p=1}^{N} (\widehat\theta_{2,p}-\theta_{2,p})^2 }. \]

docs.title: 7. Why \(SD=0.25\) will turn CAT into a four-question test
docs.text:
The narrowest prior variance is:

\[ 0.25^2 = 0.0625. \]

Its initial standard deviation \(0.25\) is already smaller than the stopping threshold \(0.3\). If there is no minimum number of questions constraint, the system may think that the accuracy is sufficient before administering the test.

Since the paper is mandatory to test at least four questions, the \(SD=0.25\) condition almost all stops immediately at the fourth question. The author makes it clear that this effectively turns the CAT into a fixed length four-question test.

Therefore, the condition "the number of questions dropped significantly to 4" cannot be interpreted as the item evidence that the measurement was completed efficiently. A more accurate explanation is:

\[ \text{Strong prior has met the accuracy requirements} \quad+\quad \text{At least four question constraints} \quad\Rightarrow\quad n=4. \]

The author also explains that \(SD=0.25\) is not the default implementation recommended in reality, but is used to show the lower limit of the number of questions that different item banks may achieve under the current stopping rule.

docs.title: 8. What is item bank well-targeted and poorly targeted?
docs.text:
PROMIS item banks generally provide higher information in locations with certain symptoms or functional impairment, and lower information in asymptomatic or ceiling/floor areas.

According to the matching degree between the real \(\theta_{2,p}\) at Time 2 and the complete item bank information function, the author divides the simulation evaluation into:

  • well-targeted: complete item bank information at the real location \(TI>22\);
  • Poorly targeted: The complete item bank information at the real location does not exceed 22.

Because:

\[ SE \approx \frac{1}{\sqrt{TI}}, \] \[ TI=22 \Rightarrow SE\approx0.21. \]

The paper chooses 22, rather than just about 11 required for \(SE=0.3\), in order to identify regions that can more stably reach the stopping condition before exhausting the item bank.

docs.title: Proportion of well-targeted items in the adult item bank
docs.text: field Proportion Physical Function 83% Fatigue 82% Ability to Participate Social 74% Sleep Disturbance 72% Anxiety 60% Depression 60% Pain Interference 60%

docs.title: Proportion of well-targeted items in children’s item bank
docs.text:
field Proportion Peer Relationships 61% Anxiety 49% Depressive Symptoms 49% Fatigue 49% Pain Interference 39% Mobility 18%

This layer cannot be used directly for real testing decisions

Well-targeted/poorly targeted are divided post hoc based on the real \(\theta_2\) in the simulation. The real location is not known before the actual CAT starts, so it is an analysis tool to explain the heterogeneity of results, not a routing rule that can be directly deployed.

docs.title: 9. Adult CAT under small changes: How much reduction in question volume
docs.text:
When \(SD(\delta)=0.3\), only the Time 2 prior mean is changed to the previous score, but \(SD=1\) is still retained. The number of questions is very close to the standard \(N(0,1)\) prior which does not use old information. The authors reported an average change of less than 0.1 question in the adult domain.

Again this says:

Moving the prior mean itself does not necessarily shorten the fixed-precision CAT; what really significantly changes the number of questions is to shrink the prior SD and let the old scores contribute more precision.

docs.title: well-targeted group
docs.text:
From prior \(SD=1\) to \(0.25\), the average number of questions dropped by about 0.44 questions across fields, ranging from:

  • Depression: dropped 0.13 questions;
  • Sleep Disturbance: Down 1.00 questions.

The benefits are limited because many well-targeted examinees only do the lowest 4 questions, and there is an obvious floor effect.

What is more practical is \(SD=0.5\):

field \(SD=1\) Question volume \(SD=0.5\) Question volume Ability to Participate Social 4.43 4.17 Anxiety 4.16 4.01 Depression 4.13 4.02 Fatigue 4.17 4.02 Pain Interference 4.49 4.31 Physical Function 4.76 4.25 Sleep Disturbance 5.00 4.16

docs.title: poorly targeted group
docs.text:
From \(SD=1\) to \(0.25\), the average reduction in all adult fields is more than 3 questions, but the reason is that CAT is forced to 4 questions.

Under the more reasonable \(SD=0.5\) conditions:

field \(SD=1\) Question volume \(SD=0.5\) Question volume Ability to Participate Social 7.72 7.34 Anxiety 7.65 7.29 Depression 7.58 7.17 Fatigue 7.13 6.16 Pain Interference 7.97 7.92 Physical Function 7.97 7.27 Sleep Disturbance 7.34 6.05

The benefit from the number of questions mainly occurs when the number of questions is close to the maximum of 8 and the item bank provides less information about the true position; however, these people are also most susceptible to the impact of wrong priors, so they cannot just look at the number of questions.

docs.title: 10. Adult CAT under small changes: How does RMSE change?
well-targeted group
docs.text:
The authors report that relative to \(SD=1\), the average RMSE improvement using informed prior is approximately:

\[ 0.025, \]

The different fields are approximately \(0.015\) to \(0.051\). Most fields get the lowest RMSE at \(SD=0.5\).

For example:

field \(SD=1\) RMSE \(SD=0.5\) RMSE \(SD=0.25\) RMSE Pain Interference 0.253 0.202 0.225 Physical Function 0.244 0.217 0.237 Sleep Disturbance 0.275 0.251 0.283

Although \(SD=0.25\) only takes 4 questions, it is already worse than \(SD=0.5\).

docs.title: poorly targeted group
docs.text:
The authors report a cross-domain average RMSE improvement of approximately:

\[ 0.059. \]

Fatigue improves the most at \(SD=0.5\), about \(0.097\):

\[ 0.407 \rightarrow 0.310. \]

But Pain Interference is an obvious counterexample:

prior SD Question volume RMSE 1.00 7.97 0.526 0.75 7.94 0.529 0.50 7.92 0.573 0.25 4.00 0.639

The stronger the prior, the shorter the question size or basically the same, but the RMSE continues to get worse. This shows that even if the true change is small overall, individual item banks and locations are still not suitable for reusing old scores.

docs.title: 11. Old scores quickly lose value when big changes occur
docs.text: The difference between the Time 1 score and the Time 2 true state is greater when \(SD(\delta)=0.8\).

docs.title: Adult well-targeted
docs.text:
The text states that only Pain Interference and Physical Function are slightly improved at \(SD=0.75\):

  • Pain Interference：RMSE \(0.276\rightarrow0.254\)；
  • Physical Function：RMSE \(0.239\rightarrow0.233\)。

The lowest RMSE for the rest of the fields generally occurs at \(SD=1\), which adds almost no additional weight to the old score.

docs.title: Adult poorly targeted
docs.text:
The text states that there are no domains where accuracy improves due to strengthening the prior. Ability to Participate Social in Table 3 is from:

\[ 0.594 \rightarrow 0.587 \]

There is a very small numerical drop at \(SD=0.75\), so "no domain improvement" should be understood as no clear or meaningful improvement, rather than a strictly monotonic worsening of each table value.

The narrowest \(SD=0.25\) reduces all tests to 4 questions and produces serious RMSE:

field \(SD=1\) RMSE \(SD=0.25\) RMSE Ability to Participate Social 0.594 0.814 Anxiety 0.516 0.775 Depression 0.518 0.761 Fatigue 0.382 0.821 Pain Interference 0.679 0.914 Physical Function 0.447 0.900 Sleep Disturbance 0.369 0.719

This is exactly the most dangerous situation in longitudinal measurements:

\[ \text{Quizzes are shorter} \quad\text{But}\quad \text{Real changes are pushed back to the old state by prior}. \]

docs.title: 12. Result of children’s item bank
docs.text: The paper only simulates small changes in the children's field \(SD(\delta)=0.3\).

docs.title: well-targeted
docs.text: The average RMSE improvement is about \(0.013\), which is smaller than the adult field. Most areas are best at \(SD=0.5\), and Mobility is slightly better at \(SD=0.75\).

docs.title: poorly targeted
docs.text:
There are only three areas with lower RMSE in \(SD=0.75\):

  • Peer Relationships；
  • Anxiety；
  • Depressive Symptoms。

Fatigue is basically unchanged, while Pain Interference and Mobility are the best at \(SD=1\). Children's item banks are smaller and ceiling/floor effects are more obvious, making prior performance more domain-dependent.

This suggests that the “best prior SD” obtained from one PROMIS domain cannot be directly generalized to other domains or age groups.

docs.title: 13. Marking issues that need attention in tables and text
13.1 Tables 2 to 4 label prior SD rows SE
docs.text:
The first column of the table is written as:

\[ SE=1,\ 0.75,\ 0.5,\ 0.25. \]

However, the methods, Figures 1 to 6, and the text all indicate that it is the prior standard deviation that is manipulated. So these lines should be as follows:

\[ SD_{\mathrm{prior}} = 1,\ 0.75,\ 0.5,\ 0.25 \]

Explanation, they cannot be read as CAT final standard error.

docs.title: 13.2 The writing method of the second parameter of \(N(0,0.3)\) is not clear enough
docs.text: In statistics, some authors use \(N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), and some use \(N(\mu,\sigma)\). This article calls 0.3 the change magnitude/effect size, and uses \(SD(\delta)\) to derive prior, so a more reasonable reading is that the standard deviation of the change is 0.3, rather than the change variance of 0.3.

docs.title: 13.3 No Monte Carlo uncertainty or significance tests reported
docs.text: The question sizes and RMSE in the table are descriptive simulation results, without confidence intervals, Monte Carlo standard errors or model comparison tests. Lower primary index values ​​for "improved" should not automatically be interpreted as stable, significant, or clinically meaningful.

docs.title: 14. Relationship with Petersen and Frans
docs.text:
Research Sources of supporting information Whether prior continues to enter the estimate Do you want to change only the first question? Main questions Petersen et al. (2026) Another HRQoL area No Yes individualized partial benefits of the first question Frans et al. (2023) oracle bias or clinical global score Yes No Risk of wrongly strong prior Bass et al. (2026) Last CAT score in the same field Yes No How to set prior SD under time change

Bass et al. are not new evidence that "external information only determines the first question", but a longitudinal version of Frans et al.: the old score changes both the initial position and the posterior accuracy and stopping time continuously.

Its unique contribution is to split the prior variance into:

\[ \text{Last scoring error} + \text{True state change variance}. \]

docs.title: 15.1 This is a simulation, not real longitudinal PROMIS data
docs.text:
Both the first and second responses were generated by the IRT model. The paper did not use repeated measures testing with real patients:

  • Whether the change distribution is truly normal; -Whether the variance is the same for different people;
  • Whether prior affects the answering behavior of real patients;
  • Whether the savings in question volume are perceptible in actual clinical practice.

docs.title: 15.2 prior mean comes from the last CAT, not user self-evaluation
docs.text:
What this article proves is:

Prior assessment information can be entered into the next CAT.

It does not demonstrate that explicit user self-assessments have the same error structure or stability.

docs.title: 15.3 well-targeted layering using real \(\theta_2\)
docs.text:
In real deployment it is not possible to know in advance which group a patient belongs to. The paper does not give an observable rule to determine:

\[ \text{The patient should use}SD=0.5 \quad\text{Still}\quad SD=1. \]

docs.title: 15.4 There is no independent separation of "first question path" and "continuous prior"
docs.text:
All Time 2 conditions allow prior to persist into EAP. The paper does not compare:

  • Select the first question using only the old score;
  • Old scores are only used for the initial EAP and are discarded after the first question;
  • Old scores persist into the full posterior.
